title: Logging Concepts and Pipeline Hygiene
html:
An analyst is only as good as the telemetry feeding the queue, and that telemetry begins as raw logs generated by hosts, network devices, applications, and cloud services. CS0-004 treats logging not as a checkbox but as an operational pipeline with distinct stages: generation, ingestion, parsing, normalization, enrichment, storage, and retention. A weakness at any stage silently degrades detection. Understanding the pipeline lets you reason about why an alert fired late, why a field is missing, or why two sources disagree about when an event happened. The analyst who cannot reason about the pipeline tends to blame the data ("the SIEM missed it") when the real fault is an upstream audit policy that was never enabled or a parser that silently dropped a malformed field.

Log ingestion and configuration

Ingestion is the act of collecting logs into a central platform, typically a SIEM or data lake. Hosts push logs with agents (the Windows Event Forwarder, Fluentd, Filebeat, or rsyslog), or the platform pulls them via APIs. Two configuration choices dominate: verbosity (which event categories are emitted, controlled by audit policies or log levels) and transport (plaintext UDP 514 syslog versus TLS-encrypted syslog over TCP 6514). Under-logging means you cannot reconstruct an incident; over-logging floods storage and buries signal. The analyst's job is to tune sources so that high-value events — authentication, process creation, privilege use, network connections — are captured reliably. On Windows this means enabling the advanced audit policy subcategories and deploying Sysmon to enrich process-creation events (Event ID 1) with hashes, command lines, and parent process. On Linux it means configuring auditd rules and ensuring application logs in /var/log ship to the collector before local rotation removes them.

Parsing and normalization mechanics

Raw logs arrive in dozens of formats: key-value pairs, CSV, JSON, free-text syslog. A parser extracts fields from each format, and normalization then maps those vendor-specific field names onto a common schema such as the Elastic Common Schema or a vendor's information model. The practical consequence is searchability: when src_ip, SourceAddress, and ip.src all resolve to one canonical field, a single query finds an indicator across every source. When parsing fails — a vendor changes its format after an upgrade, or a custom application emits an unexpected layout — the SIEM may store the event as an unparsed blob, leaving the fields you search on blank. A surprising number of "detection gaps" trace back to a broken parser rather than a missing log.

Integrity and security of logs

Logs are the primary evidence in any investigation, so attackers routinely try to delete or alter them. Log integrity controls defend against this: forwarding logs off the host in near-real time so a wiped local log still exists centrally; write-once or append-only storage (WORM); cryptographic hashing or signing of log batches; and strict access control so that only the logging service account can write to the collector. Treat the SIEM as a tier-zero asset — if an attacker owns it, they own your ability to see them. A common attacker technique is clearing the Windows Security log (Event ID 1102 is itself logged when this happens) or stopping the logging service; off-host forwarding ensures the evidence survives even when the local copy is destroyed.

Time synchronization

Correlating events across dozens of sources is impossible if their clocks disagree. NTP (Network Time Protocol) synchronizes system clocks to a common reference, and analysts strongly prefer that all logs be normalized to UTC to eliminate time-zone ambiguity during cross-region investigations. A host whose clock has drifted by minutes will scatter its events across the timeline, breaking the cause-and-effect chain you rely on. When building an incident timeline, the analyst converts every timestamp to a single zone (UTC) and notes whether a source records local time, server-receipt time, or both — the gap between event time and ingestion time can itself be an indicator of buffering or a stalled forwarder.

Pipeline stageWhat happensCommon failure
GenerationSource emits an eventAudit policy disabled — event never created
IngestionAgent or API delivers logUDP syslog silently dropped under load
ParsingFields extracted from raw textFormat change breaks parser, fields blank
NormalizationFields mapped to common schemaCustom format unmapped, search misses it
EnrichmentContext added (GeoIP, reputation)Stale intel feed, missing asset data
RetentionStored for a defined windowLogs rotated out before investigation

Retention and storage tiers

Retention defines how long logs are kept and is driven by regulation, contract, and threat-detection reality. Many breaches have a long dwell time — the attacker is present for months before discovery — so a 30-day retention window can mean the initial intrusion logs are already gone when you finally investigate. Common drivers include PCI DSS (one year, with 90 days immediately available) and HIPAA. Analysts balance cost against the need to look backward, often using tiered storage: recent logs stay in hot, searchable storage, while older logs move to cheaper cold or archival storage that is slower to query but still available for retrospective hunting. The decision of what to keep hot versus cold is itself a detection-strategy choice.

A practical ingestion checklist keeps the pipeline healthy and prevents the silent gaps that masquerade as detection failures:

  • Confirm audit policy is enabled at the source before trusting that events exist.
  • Prefer TLS syslog over TCP 6514 to plaintext UDP 514 so logs are not silently dropped under load.
  • Forward logs off-host in near-real time so a wiped local log still exists centrally.
  • Monitor parser health after every vendor upgrade — a format change can blank the fields you search on.
  • Normalize every timestamp to UTC and verify NTP synchronization across all sources.
Storage tierSpeedTypical window
HotInstant search30–90 days
WarmMinutes to query90 days–1 year
Cold / archiveRestore required1–7 years (compliance)
Normalization vs enrichment

Normalization maps disparate vendor fields into one schema (so src_ip, SourceAddress, and ip.src all become one searchable field). Enrichment adds context the raw log lacked — GeoIP, asset owner, threat-intel reputation. Normalization makes search possible; enrichment makes triage fast.

Exam tip

If a question describes events from two systems that "do not line up" or an attacker "clearing logs," the answer almost always involves time synchronization (NTP/UTC) or log integrity / off-host forwarding, respectively. Map the symptom to the pipeline stage.

Scenario

A SOC finds the attacker was active for 95 days, but the SIEM only holds 30 days of firewall logs. The earliest intrusion evidence is unrecoverable. The deliverable is a retention-policy change extending firewall and authentication logs to one year — a direct response to observed dwell time — paired with a tiered-storage design so the cost stays manageable.

title: Operating System Concepts: Hardening, File Systems, and Processes
html:
Analysts spend their days reading host evidence, so a working mental model of how operating systems are structured — and how they should be locked down — is essential. This section covers system hardening, the file-system layouts of Windows and Linux, the files attackers and defenders care about most, and the legitimate system processes you must recognize so that the malicious imposters stand out. Every triage decision an analyst makes rests on an internal sense of what "normal" looks like for the platform; without it, ordinary system behavior reads as suspicious and genuine attacks blend in.

System hardening

Hardening reduces a system's attack surface by removing or disabling everything not required for its role. The core steps are consistent across platforms: remove unnecessary software and services, close unused ports, disable default and guest accounts, enforce least privilege, apply a secure configuration baseline (often from CIS Benchmarks or DISA STIGs), enable host firewalls and disk encryption, and keep patches current. Hardening is preventive; logging and EDR are detective. A hardened host gives the attacker fewer footholds and the analyst fewer noisy services to triage. CIS Benchmarks provide prescriptive, numbered settings (for example, "ensure SMBv1 is disabled") and many tools can scan a host and report a compliance percentage against the benchmark, giving the SOC a measurable hardening posture rather than a vague assertion that systems are "locked down."

Configuration baselines and drift

A hardened state is not permanent. Over time, administrators install software, change settings for troubleshooting, and grant temporary exceptions that never get removed — this is configuration drift. The analyst's interest is twofold: drift widens the attack surface, and a sudden deviation from baseline (a firewall rule disabled, audit logging turned off, a new service installed) can itself be an indicator of compromise. Tooling that continuously compares live configuration against the approved baseline turns drift into an alert. This is why hardening and detection are linked: the same baseline that reduces attack surface also defines the "normal" that anomaly detection measures against.

Windows vs Linux file structure

Windows organizes files under drive letters with system binaries in C:\Windows\System32, per-user data under C:\Users, and configuration in the Registry rather than flat files. Linux uses a single rooted tree (/) following the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: binaries in /bin and /usr/bin, configuration in /etc, user homes in /home, runtime state in /var, and volatile process/kernel data exposed under /proc. The /proc filesystem is especially valuable in live response: /proc/<pid>/exe reveals the on-disk path of a running process even if the binary was deleted, and /proc/<pid>/cmdline shows the full invocation — the Linux equivalent of reading a Windows process's command line.

PurposeWindowsLinux
System binariesC:\Windows\System32/bin, /sbin, /usr/bin
ConfigurationRegistry (HKLM, HKCU)/etc
Accounts / credentialsSAM hive, NTDS.dit (DC)/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow
User dataC:\Users\<name>/home/<name>
LogsEVTX (Event Viewer)/var/log
Scheduled tasksTask Scheduler, schtaskscron, systemd timers

Critical files to know

On Linux, /etc/passwd lists accounts and /etc/shadow stores password hashes; /etc/sudoers governs privilege escalation; ~/.ssh/authorized_keys grants key-based access (a classic persistence target); and cron files under /etc/cron* schedule tasks (another persistence spot). On Windows, the SAM and NTDS.dit hold credential material, the hosts file can hijack name resolution, and autorun Registry keys (Run, RunOnce) establish persistence. An analyst investigating a possible foothold checks these locations first because they are where attackers reliably plant the mechanisms that survive a reboot — a new line in authorized_keys, an extra entry in a Run key, or a fresh account in /etc/passwd with UID 0.

A first-pass foothold check walks these high-value locations in order:

  1. New or modified accounts (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, local administrators).
  2. Autorun and persistence entries (Run/RunOnce keys, services, scheduled tasks, cron).
  3. SSH trust (~/.ssh/authorized_keys) and sudo rights (/etc/sudoers).
  4. Name-resolution tampering (the hosts file) and credential stores (SAM, NTDS.dit).

System processes

Recognizing legitimate Windows processes lets you spot fakes. System (PID 4), smss.exe, csrss.exe, wininit.exe, services.exe, lsass.exe, and svchost.exe have known parents, paths, and counts. A lsass.exe running from a user's Temp folder, or a second copy spawned by Word, is almost certainly malware impersonating a trusted name. The analyst's mental model is a tree: System spawns smss.exe, which launches csrss.exe and wininit.exe; wininit.exe launches services.exe and lsass.exe; and services.exe launches the many svchost.exe instances. Any branch that violates this tree is suspect.

ProcessLegit parentLegit path / count
lsass.exewininit.exeSystem32, single instance
svchost.exeservices.exeSystem32, many instances
csrss.exesmss.exe (exits)System32, one per session
explorer.exeuserinit.exeC:\Windows, per user
Known-good anchors

lsass.exe runs once, from System32, parented by wininit.exe. svchost.exe runs many times but always parented by services.exe and always from System32. Memorize the legitimate parent/path so deviations jump out.

Exam tip

A process with a trusted name (svchost, lsass) but the wrong parent process or wrong file path is the textbook indicator of masquerading malware. Path and parentage beat name every time.

Scenario

EDR flags svch0st.exe (zero, not letter o) running from C:\Users\Public with no parent in the services tree. The name is a near-miss of a trusted binary and the path is wrong — a clear masquerading indicator. The analyst isolates the host and pulls the binary for analysis rather than dismissing it as a normal service host.

title: Infrastructure and System Architecture
html:
Modern environments are rarely a rack of physical servers. They are layered abstractions — virtual machines, containers, serverless functions, and managed cloud services — and each layer changes where logs live, who is responsible for security, and how an attacker moves. An analyst must know these architectures cold to interpret telemetry correctly, because the same alert means different things depending on whether it came from a long-lived VM, an ephemeral container, or a serverless function that existed for 200 milliseconds.

Virtualization

Virtualization runs multiple guest operating systems on one physical host via a hypervisor. A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor such as ESXi or Hyper-V runs directly on hardware and is used in data centers; a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor such as VirtualBox runs atop a host OS for desktop use. The security concern unique to virtualization is VM escape — breaking out of a guest to attack the hypervisor or sibling VMs — and resource contention used as a covert side channel. The hypervisor itself becomes a high-value target: compromising it grants control of every guest, so analysts treat hypervisor logs and management-plane access (vCenter, the Hyper-V host) with the same care as a domain controller.

Containerization

Containers (Docker, containerd) package an application with its dependencies and share the host kernel rather than booting a full OS, making them lightweight and fast. Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale. Because containers share a kernel, a kernel exploit or a misconfigured privileged container can compromise the host and every sibling. Image hygiene matters: a vulnerable base image, embedded secrets, or a poisoned public registry image are recurring attack vectors. Containers are also ephemeral — a compromised container may be destroyed and recreated in seconds, which means forensic evidence vanishes unless logs and process telemetry are shipped off the container in real time. The analyst's challenge shifts from imaging a disk to capturing volatile, short-lived state.

ModelIsolation boundaryKey risk
Virtual machineHypervisor / full guest OSVM escape
ContainerShared kernel + namespacesKernel escape, image poisoning
ServerlessProvider-managed runtimeOver-permissioned function role
Bare metalPhysical hardwareFirmware / supply-chain implant

Cloud-native technologies

Cloud-native design favors small, independently deployable microservices communicating over APIs, with serverless functions (Lambda, Azure Functions) executing code on demand without managed servers. This shifts the security focus: there is no host to patch, so the analyst watches API gateways, identity roles attached to functions, and inter-service traffic. An over-permissioned IAM role on a serverless function is the cloud equivalent of an over-privileged service account — if the function is compromised through a vulnerable dependency, the attacker inherits whatever the role can do, which in a poorly scoped environment may be read access to every storage bucket.

Infrastructure as Code and immutable infrastructure

Cloud-native environments are typically defined in Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, CloudFormation), which means the security posture of an entire fleet is determined by a few template files. This is a double-edged property: a single misconfigured template — a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0, logging disabled by default — replicates the flaw across every deployment, but it also means a fix applied to the template fixes everything at once. Many cloud-native shops practice immutable infrastructure, where servers are never patched in place but replaced wholesale from a new image. For the analyst this changes response: you do not clean a compromised instance, you terminate it and let the orchestrator launch a known-good replacement, capturing forensic data first.

When triaging an alert, the abstraction layer changes what evidence even exists and how fast it disappears:

  • Long-lived VM: disk and memory imaging are viable; treat like a traditional host.
  • Container: ship process and network telemetry off-host in real time — the container may vanish in seconds.
  • Serverless function: rely on control-plane and invocation logs; there is no host to image.
  • Managed service: the only evidence is the provider's audit trail, so confirm it is enabled first.

The shared responsibility model

In cloud, security duties split between provider and customer. The provider secures the underlying infrastructure; the customer secures their data, identities, and configurations. The split shifts by service model: with IaaS the customer patches the guest OS, while with SaaS the provider handles nearly everything except access and data governance. Misreading this boundary is a leading cause of cloud breaches — teams assume the provider "handles security" and leave a storage bucket world-readable or never configure logging on a managed service.

ModelCustomer securesProvider secures
IaaSOS, apps, data, IAMHypervisor, hardware, network
PaaSApps, data, IAMOS, runtime, infrastructure
SaaSData, access governanceNearly everything else
API as attack surface

Microservice and serverless architectures expose far more APIs than monolithic apps. Broken object-level authorization, missing rate limiting, and excessive data exposure (the OWASP API Top 10) are now front-line analyst concerns, not just developer ones.

Exam tip

Match the abstraction to its signature risk: VM → escape; container → shared-kernel / image compromise; serverless → over-permissioned role. And know that responsibility shifts toward the customer as you move IaaS → PaaS → SaaS.

Scenario

A vulnerable dependency in a Lambda function is exploited. Because the function's IAM role had a wildcard s3:* permission, the attacker reads every bucket in the account. The fix is least-privilege scoping of the function role plus enabling control-plane logging — not patching a server that does not exist.

title: Network Architecture and Zero Trust
html:
The defensible perimeter is gone. Users connect from anywhere, workloads live in multiple clouds, and the classic castle-and-moat model assumes trust the moment a device is "inside." Modern network architecture replaces implicit trust with continuous verification, and the analyst must understand the controls that enforce it — both to interpret where telemetry comes from and to recommend the right control when an investigation reveals that lateral movement was too easy.

Network segmentation

Segmentation divides a network into zones (VLANs, subnets, security groups) so that a compromise in one zone cannot freely reach another. Microsegmentation takes this to the workload level, applying per-host or per-application policy. Segmentation is the single most effective control against lateral movement — the attacker behavior of pivoting from the initially compromised host toward high-value targets. A well-segmented network forces the attacker to cross policy-enforced boundaries that generate logs and alerts each time, converting silent movement into observable events. Flat networks, by contrast, let an attacker who lands on a single workstation reach the database tier, the backup server, and the domain controller with nothing in the way.

Zero Trust and ZTNA

Zero Trust operates on "never trust, always verify": every request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted regardless of source location, and access is granted least-privilege and re-evaluated continuously. The architecture splits decision-making into a policy decision point (which evaluates identity, device posture, and context) and a policy enforcement point (which allows or blocks the connection). ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) implements this for remote access, replacing the broad network tunnel of a traditional VPN with brokered, per-application access. A user authenticated to one app gains no implicit reach to others. The practical difference from a VPN is profound: a VPN places the device on the network and trusts it thereafter, while ZTNA brokers each application session and continuously re-checks posture, so a compromised endpoint cannot use its connection as a launchpad to scan the internal network.

ConceptWhat it doesAnalyst relevance
SegmentationIsolates network zonesLimits lateral movement
ZTNAPer-app brokered accessReplaces flat VPN trust
CASBVisibility/control over SaaSDetects shadow IT, enforces DLP
SASEConverged network + security edgeSingle policy point for distributed users
SWGFilters/inspects web trafficBlocks malicious sites, logs egress

SASE and CASB

SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) converges networking (SD-WAN) and security services (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) into one cloud-delivered platform, applying consistent policy to users wherever they are. A CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) sits between users and cloud services to give visibility into SaaS usage, detect shadow IT, enforce DLP, and flag risky configurations. For an analyst, the CASB is often the only source of telemetry on sanctioned-and-unsanctioned cloud app activity — it can reveal that employees are uploading documents to an unapproved file-sharing service, or that a sanctioned app has a sharing setting exposing data publicly. Because SASE centralizes egress through a cloud edge, it also becomes a single, rich logging point for everything users do on the internet.

Defense in depth and the modern edge

No single control is sufficient, so architectures layer them — this is defense in depth. A secure web gateway inspects and filters outbound web traffic, a next-generation firewall enforces application-aware rules, an IPS blocks known exploit patterns, and DNS filtering stops connections to malicious domains before a packet even leaves. For the analyst, each layer is both a control and a sensor: a blocked connection at the SWG is also a log entry that may be the first sign of malware attempting to reach its command-and-control server. Understanding the layering lets you trace an attack across controls and identify which layer caught it and which let it through.

Hybrid cloud

A hybrid cloud combines on-premises infrastructure with one or more public clouds, connected by VPN or dedicated links. The security challenge is consistency: identity, logging, and policy must span both environments, and the seams between them — federation trust, network peering — are prime targets. Centralized log aggregation across the hybrid boundary is what lets an analyst follow an attacker who pivots from cloud to on-prem. A common failure is that on-prem and cloud are monitored by separate teams with separate tools, so an attacker crossing the boundary disappears from one team's view and reappears in another's with no correlation between them.

TraitTraditional VPNZTNA
Trust modelAuthenticate once, trust thereafterContinuous per-request verification
Access scopeBroad network reachPer-application brokered
Device postureChecked at connect (if at all)Re-evaluated every session
Lateral movementCompromised endpoint can scan internallyNo implicit path between apps

When an investigation shows movement was too easy, the analyst's recommendation usually walks this layered ladder:

  1. Segment the network into zones so a compromise cannot freely cross tiers.
  2. Apply microsegmentation at the workload level for high-value assets.
  3. Replace flat VPN access with ZTNA brokered per application.
  4. Centralize egress and logging through a SASE edge for distributed users.
VPN vs ZTNA

A VPN authenticates once and drops the device onto the network with broad reach. ZTNA brokers access per application and continuously re-evaluates identity and device posture. "Replace the VPN so a compromised laptop cannot scan the internal network" is the textbook ZTNA driver.

Scenario

An attacker compromises one workstation and immediately tries to RDP to the database server. Because the network was flat, the attempt succeeds. The remediation is microsegmentation plus ZTNA so the workstation has no implicit path to the database tier — lateral movement is denied by default and each cross-zone attempt generates an alert.

Exam tip

"Never trust, always verify" and "continuous authentication" point to Zero Trust. "Per-application remote access replacing VPN" is ZTNA. "Visibility into SaaS / shadow IT" is CASB. "Converged cloud-delivered network + security" is SASE.

title: Identity and Access Management in Security Operations
html:
Identity is the new perimeter. With workloads dispersed across clouds and the network boundary dissolved, most attacks ultimately turn on stealing, forging, or abusing an identity. The analyst must understand how identities are proven, how access is granted, and where the high-value secrets live — because a large share of modern detections are identity-centric: anomalous logins, token abuse, privilege escalation, and credential theft.

Identity and authentication

An identity is a unique representation of a user, service, or device. Authentication proves the identity using one or more factors: something you know (password), something you have (token, phone), something you are (biometric), and contextually somewhere you are or something you do. Combining categories yields MFA. Note that two passwords are not MFA — they are the same factor twice. Phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys defeat the credential-replay attacks that plague SMS and push-based MFA, because the cryptographic challenge is bound to the legitimate site's origin and cannot be relayed by a proxy phishing page. Analysts increasingly see attackers bypass weaker MFA through real-time proxy kits that capture the session cookie after a successful push, which is why token-theft detection matters even when MFA is enabled.

Federation and SSO

Federation lets an identity from one trust domain be accepted by another, enabling single sign-on across organizations and SaaS apps using standards such as SAML and OpenID Connect (OIDC), with OAuth 2.0 handling delegated authorization. The identity provider (IdP) authenticates once and issues signed tokens the service provider trusts. For analysts, a forged or stolen SAML token (the "Golden SAML" attack) lets an adversary impersonate any user without touching the password — a key cloud-era detection target. The defensive implication is that the IdP and its token-signing keys are tier-zero assets: whoever controls the signing certificate can mint valid tokens for any user, so monitoring IdP configuration changes and unusual token issuance is essential.

StandardPrimary purpose
SAMLWeb SSO via XML assertions
OIDCAuthentication layer on OAuth 2.0
OAuth 2.0Delegated authorization (access tokens)
KerberosOn-prem AD ticket-based auth
LDAPDirectory lookup / bind authentication

Authorization models

After authentication, authorization decides what the identity may do. Common models are RBAC (permissions by role), ABAC (permissions by attributes/context), and least privilege applied throughout. Mandatory and discretionary access control round out the set. The analyst watches for privilege creep and for accounts that suddenly exercise rights outside their role. RBAC is simple to audit because permissions cluster around roles, but it tends toward role explosion and creep over time; ABAC is more expressive — granting access based on department, location, time, and device posture simultaneously — at the cost of greater complexity and harder auditing.

ModelBasis for accessTrade-off
RBACAssigned roleSimple, but role creep
ABACAttributes / contextFlexible, complex to audit
MACSystem-enforced labelsRigid, high assurance
DACOwner discretionFlexible, prone to sprawl

PAM and secrets management

Privileged Access Management (PAM) controls administrative accounts with vaulting, session recording, just-in-time elevation, and credential rotation, shrinking the window in which a stolen admin password is useful. Secrets management tools (HashiCorp Vault, cloud KMS) store API keys, certificates, and service credentials out of source code and inject them at runtime. Hard-coded secrets in a Git repository are one of the most common — and most preventable — initial-access vectors, because public and even private repos are routinely scraped for keys, and a single leaked cloud access key can lead to full account compromise within minutes of being committed.

Service and machine identities

Human users are no longer the majority of identities in most environments. Service accounts, API keys, managed identities, and certificates outnumber people, and they are frequently over-privileged, rarely rotated, and poorly monitored. Attackers prize them because their use rarely triggers MFA and their activity blends into automated noise. The analyst should treat a service account authenticating from an unusual host, at an unusual time, or performing an action outside its normal pattern as a high-priority anomaly — these accounts have predictable behavior, which makes deviation a strong signal.

The authentication factor categories the exam tests, with the rule that combining different categories — not repeating one — yields MFA:

  • Something you know — password, PIN, security question.
  • Something you have — hardware token, phone, smart card, FIDO2 key.
  • Something you are — fingerprint, face, or other biometric.
  • Somewhere you are / something you do — location or behavioral context.
Why PAM matters to the SOC

Privileged accounts are the attacker's goal, not just a step. Session recording and JIT elevation turn a normally invisible admin action into a reviewable, time-boxed event — converting a blind spot into telemetry.

Exam tip

"Two passwords" is single-factor. "Token without touching the password" suggests federation/SAML abuse. "Hard-coded API key in code" → secrets management. "Vault, JIT elevation, session recording for admins" → PAM.

Scenario

A backup service account that normally runs only on the backup server at 2 a.m. authenticates interactively from a workstation at midday and accesses a file share it never touches. Because service accounts have predictable behavior, this deviation is a high-fidelity sign of credential theft — the analyst disables the account and hunts for how the credential leaked.

title: Encryption Techniques and Data Protection
html:
Cryptography underpins confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. An analyst does not need to implement ciphers, but must recognize which technique solves which problem, and must understand data-protection controls well enough to interpret DLP alerts and assess whether stolen data was actually exposed. The recurring analyst question — "was this data readable to the attacker?" — depends entirely on whether and how it was encrypted, and on whether the attacker also obtained the key.

Symmetric encryption

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encryption and decryption. AES (128/256-bit) is the standard; it is fast and suited to bulk data — full-disk encryption, database encryption, TLS session traffic. Its weakness is key distribution: every party needs the same secret, so getting the key to them safely is the hard part. The mode of operation matters too: AES-GCM provides both confidentiality and integrity (authenticated encryption), while older modes like ECB leak patterns and should never appear in a secure design — recognizing that an application uses a weak mode is a legitimate finding in a security review.

Asymmetric encryption

Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked key pair — a public key anyone may hold and a private key the owner guards. RSA and ECC are the common algorithms. It solves key distribution and enables digital signatures, but it is slow, so in practice it is used to exchange a symmetric session key (hybrid encryption, as in TLS) rather than to encrypt bulk data directly. A digital signature reverses the key roles: the sender signs with their private key and anyone verifies with the public key, proving both integrity and authenticity (non-repudiation). This is the mechanism behind code signing, signed email (S/MIME), and the certificates that anchor TLS.

Hashing

Hashing is a one-way function producing a fixed-length digest used to verify integrity, not to conceal data. SHA-256 is the modern default; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security use due to collisions. Passwords are stored as salted hashes using slow, memory-hard functions such as bcrypt or Argon2 to resist cracking. A hash proves data is unchanged; it cannot be reversed to recover the input. The salt — a unique random value per password — defeats precomputed rainbow tables and ensures two users with the same password produce different hashes. In forensics and malware analysis, hashes also serve as identifiers: a file's SHA-256 is its fingerprint for threat-intel lookups.

GoalTechniqueExample
Bulk confidentialitySymmetricAES-256
Key exchange / signaturesAsymmetricRSA, ECC
Integrity verificationHashingSHA-256
Password storageSalted slow hashbcrypt, Argon2
Message authenticityHMAC / signatureHMAC-SHA256

PKI and certificates

Public Key Infrastructure ties public keys to identities through certificates issued by a trusted Certificate Authority. A certificate binds a key to a name and is itself signed by the CA, creating a chain of trust up to a root the system already trusts. Analysts encounter PKI constantly: an expired certificate breaks a service, a self-signed certificate on a login page is a phishing indicator, and certificate transparency logs can reveal an attacker who registered a lookalike domain and obtained a certificate for it. Revocation (CRL and OCSP) lets a compromised certificate be invalidated before it expires — relevant whenever a private key is suspected stolen.

Data protection fundamentals

Data exists in three states: at rest (storage, protected by disk/DB encryption), in transit (network, protected by TLS), and in use (memory, the hardest to protect, addressed by confidential-computing enclaves). Other controls include tokenization (replacing sensitive values with non-sensitive surrogates), masking (hiding part of a value, such as showing only the last four digits of a card), and classification/labeling that drives how each category is handled. The state of the data dictates the control: TLS does nothing for data sitting decrypted in a database, and disk encryption does nothing for data moving over the wire.

Data statePrimary controlExample
At restDisk / database encryptionBitLocker, TDE
In transitTransport encryptionTLS 1.3, IPsec
In useConfidential computingEnclaves (SGX/SEV)

When assessing whether stolen data was truly exposed, the analyst works through a short decision sequence:

  1. Was the data encrypted in the state it was stolen from (at rest, in transit, in use)?
  2. Did the attacker also obtain the decryption key or an active session?
  3. Was the algorithm and mode strong (AES-GCM) rather than broken (ECB, MD5)?
  4. Only if all protections held can exposure be ruled out for notification purposes.

Data Loss Prevention

DLP systems inspect data in motion (email, web uploads), at rest (file shares), and at the endpoint (USB, clipboard) to detect and block unauthorized exfiltration of sensitive content, identified by patterns (credit-card regex), exact-match fingerprints, or classification labels. Tuning DLP is an analyst task: too strict and it blocks legitimate work; too loose and real exfiltration slips through. DLP also pairs with classification — a document labeled "Confidential" can be automatically blocked from leaving the organization, turning a policy label into an enforced control.

Encryption does not equal exposure

If stolen data was strong-encrypted and the attacker never obtained the key, the data is not meaningfully exposed — a critical distinction in breach assessment and notification decisions. Always ask: did the attacker get the key, too?

Exam tip

If a scenario asks how to verify a file was not altered, the answer is hashing, never encryption. If it asks to protect bulk data on disk, that is symmetric/AES. If it asks to exchange a key or prove identity, that is asymmetric.

Scenario

A laptop is stolen. Investigation confirms the disk was protected with AES full-disk encryption and the key was never extracted. The analyst documents that the data was not exposed, which materially changes the breach-notification obligation compared with an unencrypted drive.

title: Critical Infrastructure: OT, ICS, and SCADA
html:
Industrial environments — power grids, water treatment, manufacturing lines, pipelines — run on technology with priorities inverted from ordinary IT. Where IT prioritizes confidentiality, operational technology prioritizes availability and safety: a process that controls a turbine cannot simply reboot for a patch. Analysts assigned to these environments must adjust both their threat model and their tooling, because techniques that are routine in enterprise IT — active scanning, forced patching, agent deployment — can disrupt or even destroy fragile control systems.

OT, ICS, and SCADA defined

Operational Technology (OT) is hardware and software that monitors or controls physical processes. Industrial Control Systems (ICS) is the umbrella term for the control components — programmable logic controllers (PLCs), remote terminal units (RTUs), and human-machine interfaces (HMIs). SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) is a class of ICS that centrally monitors and controls geographically dispersed assets, such as a utility's substations across a region. A PLC executes the control logic (open a valve when a tank reaches a level); an HMI is the operator's screen; and the SCADA system aggregates many sites into a central control room. Understanding which component does what tells the analyst where an attacker who manipulated a physical process would have had to operate.

TermScopeExample component
OTTech controlling physical processesSensors, actuators
ICSControl-system umbrellaPLC, RTU, HMI
SCADADispersed supervisory controlPipeline / grid monitoring
DCSSingle-facility process controlRefinery, chemical plant

Why OT security is different

OT devices are long-lived (20+ year service life), often run unpatched embedded operating systems, and speak specialized protocols — Modbus, DNP3, PROFINET — that were designed for trusted serial links and frequently lack authentication or encryption. Active scanning that is routine in IT can crash a fragile PLC, so analysts favor passive monitoring. The consequence of compromise is physical: equipment damage, environmental release, or loss of life, not just data loss. Modbus, for example, has no concept of authentication — any device that can reach a PLC on the network can issue a command to write a register, which is why network reachability to OT devices is itself the primary risk to control.

Securing OT

The dominant control is segmentation following the Purdue Model, which layers the enterprise into levels and inserts a demilitarized zone between IT and OT so that no direct path exists from the corporate network to a controller. Other controls include unidirectional gateways (data diodes) that allow monitoring traffic out but no commands in, strict allow-listing, and passive network monitoring with OT-aware sensors. The Stuxnet worm and the Ukrainian grid attacks are the canonical case studies of what OT compromise looks like — Stuxnet specifically reprogrammed PLCs while feeding operators normal readings, illustrating why integrity of control logic matters as much as availability.

The IT/OT convergence problem

Historically OT networks were physically isolated ("air-gapped"), but business demand for remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, and data analytics has connected them to IT and the internet, eroding that isolation. This IT/OT convergence is the root of most modern OT risk: a path now often exists from a phishing email on the corporate network to a controller that was never designed to be reachable. Jump hosts, vendor remote-access tools, and shared Active Directory between IT and OT are the typical bridges attackers exploit. The analyst's job is to inventory and monitor every one of these crossing points, because the air gap that the OT team assumes still exists frequently does not.

Monitoring OT without breaking it

Because agents and active probes are risky, OT monitoring leans on passive techniques: a network tap or SPAN port feeds an OT-aware sensor (such as those that parse Modbus and DNP3) which builds an asset inventory and a baseline of normal command patterns purely by observation. Any new device, any unexpected command (a write to a controller that historically only received reads), or a connection from the IT side crossing the DMZ becomes an alert. The analyst's goal is full visibility with zero interference — observe everything, touch nothing — which is the opposite of the agent-heavy, actively scanned IT model.

OT controlPurposeIT contrast
Purdue-model segmentationNo direct IT-to-controller pathFlatter, identity-gated zones
Unidirectional gateway (data diode)Monitoring out, no commands inBidirectional firewalls
Passive monitoring (SPAN/tap)Visibility with zero interferenceActive scanning, agents
Allow-listingOnly known commands permittedDeny-list / signature blocking

Before any monitoring touches an OT network, the analyst follows safety-first rules:

  • Never actively scan a live controller — a fragile PLC can lock up and halt production.
  • Use passive capture from a SPAN port or tap, not host agents.
  • Deploy OT-aware sensors that parse Modbus and DNP3 to baseline normal commands.
  • Alert on any write to a controller that historically only received reads.
  • Inventory and watch every IT/OT crossing point, since the assumed air gap often does not exist.
The CIA priority flip

In IT the usual priority is Confidentiality > Integrity > Availability. In OT it inverts to Availability and safety first, then Integrity, then Confidentiality. This flip drives every design choice — including why you may not patch immediately.

Exam tip

OT clues: Modbus/DNP3, PLC/HMI/SCADA, "cannot take the process offline," "passive monitoring," "Purdue model." The right control is usually segmentation / data diode / passive monitoring, not aggressive scanning or forced patching.

Scenario

A new vulnerability scanner is pointed at a plant network and a PLC controlling a mixing process locks up, halting production. The lesson and remediation: OT requires passive monitoring and a Purdue-segmented network, never active scanning of live controllers. The analyst recommends an OT-aware passive sensor on a SPAN port instead.

title: Device and Endpoint Management
html:
Endpoints — laptops, phones, tablets, kiosks, IoT — are where users work and where most intrusions begin. Managing them at scale, enforcing configuration, and retaining the ability to respond remotely are core security-operations capabilities. CS0-004 expects familiarity with the management platforms and the mobile-specific controls, because the same endpoint management infrastructure that keeps devices patched is also the analyst's primary lever for containment during an incident.

Endpoint management

Unified endpoint management platforms push configuration baselines, deploy and patch software, enforce encryption, and report compliance status. They give the SOC two things: posture visibility (which endpoints are unpatched, unencrypted, or non-compliant) and a remote response lever (push a patch, isolate a host, wipe a stolen device). An asset inventory built from endpoint management is a prerequisite for any meaningful vulnerability or incident program — you cannot defend what you do not know exists. During an active incident, the same platform that normally pushes software can push an emergency patch or a containment configuration to thousands of hosts in minutes, which is why integrating endpoint management with the incident-response workflow pays off precisely when it matters most.

Mobile Device Management

MDM enforces policy on smartphones and tablets: passcode requirements, encryption, remote lock and wipe, app allow/deny lists, and certificate distribution. Two enrollment philosophies dominate. COPE (corporate-owned, personally enabled) gives the organization full control of a company device. BYOD (bring your own device) uses personal hardware, which forces a privacy-versus-control compromise. MDM is itself a high-value target: because it can push configuration and apps to every enrolled device, an attacker who compromises the MDM console could deploy malware fleet-wide, so the management platform deserves the same tier-zero protection as a domain controller or SIEM.

ModelOwnershipControl trade-off
COPECorporateFull control, some personal use allowed
BYODEmployeeLimited control; privacy concerns
CYODCorporate (user-chosen)Full control, user picks model
COBOCorporate (locked down)Single-purpose, no personal use

Containerization on mobile

To reconcile BYOD privacy with corporate control, MDM uses containerization — a managed, encrypted workspace on the device that holds corporate apps and data separately from personal content. The organization can selectively wipe only the corporate container when an employee leaves, without touching personal photos. This is the standard answer to "how do we protect company data on a personal phone without invading privacy." The container also enforces its own policies — copy/paste restrictions between corporate and personal apps, mandatory encryption, separate authentication — so corporate data cannot trivially leak into a personal cloud backup.

IoT and embedded device risk

Beyond traditional endpoints, the network increasingly hosts IoT and embedded devices — cameras, sensors, badge readers, smart-building controllers — that often ship with default credentials, rarely receive patches, and have no agent the SOC can install. These devices expand the attack surface and are favored as footholds and as nodes in botnets. The analyst's strategy mirrors OT: segment them onto isolated VLANs, monitor their traffic passively for anomalies, change default credentials, and treat any of them initiating unexpected outbound connections as suspicious, since a camera should never be talking to a host in another country.

Mobile threats and controls

Mobile-specific risks include sideloaded malicious apps, jailbreaking/rooting that disables built-in protections, insecure public Wi-Fi, and SMS phishing (smishing). Controls include app vetting and allow-listing, jailbreak/root detection, mandatory VPN, and conditional access that blocks non-compliant devices from corporate resources. Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) agents extend EDR-like detection to phones, watching for malicious apps, network attacks, and OS exploits that the MDM's configuration enforcement alone would miss. The split is worth remembering: MDM enforces configuration (passcode, encryption, allow-lists), while MTD detects threats in real time the way EDR does on a laptop — an organization with strict MDM policy can still be compromised by a zero-day exploit that only MTD behavioral detection would catch.

Conditional access

Conditional access ties resource access to device and identity posture: only a device that is enrolled, encrypted, patched to a minimum OS, and not jailbroken may reach corporate email or applications, and the check happens at every connection rather than once at enrollment. This converts the MDM's compliance data into an enforcement gate — a phone that falls out of compliance (root detected, OS downgraded) is automatically blocked until remediated. For the analyst, conditional-access denials are also telemetry: a normally compliant device suddenly failing posture checks can indicate tampering, and a sudden spike in denials across many users may signal a misconfigured policy or an attacker probing with non-compliant devices.

A conditional-access gate typically requires a device to satisfy every posture check before it reaches corporate resources:

  • Enrolled in MDM and reporting compliance.
  • Disk encryption enabled.
  • Patched to a minimum OS version.
  • Not jailbroken or rooted.
  • Passing real-time MTD threat checks where deployed.
Mobile riskControl
Sideloaded malwareApp allow-list, MTD
Jailbreak / rootCompliance check, conditional access
Data leakage from BYODContainerization, selective wipe
SmishingUser training, URL filtering
Scenario

An employee on a BYOD phone resigns. Security must remove company email and files but cannot wipe the personal device. MDM performs a selective wipe of the corporate container only, satisfying both the data-protection and the privacy requirement.

Exam tip

"Protect company data on a personal phone without touching personal data" → containerization + selective wipe. "Block unpatched/jailbroken devices from corporate apps" → conditional access via MDM.

title: Network-Related Indicators of Malicious Activity
html:
Network telemetry is often where an intrusion first becomes visible, because attackers must eventually communicate — to a command-and-control server, between footholds, or out to an exfiltration endpoint. CS0-004 objective 1.2 asks you to recognize the network indicators that betray each of these behaviors. The unifying skill is comparing observed traffic against an established baseline: nearly every network indicator is fundamentally a deviation from how a host or network normally behaves.

Reconnaissance: scanning and enumeration

Before attacking, adversaries map the environment. Scanning probes ranges of hosts and ports to find live systems and open services; enumeration goes deeper, extracting usernames, shares, and software versions from those services. On the wire these show as a single source touching many destinations or ports in a short window, lots of SYN packets without completed handshakes (a SYN scan), or repeated queries to directory services. Sequential or fan-out connection patterns are the tell. A horizontal scan touches one port across many hosts (hunting for a specific vulnerable service); a vertical scan touches many ports on one host (profiling a single target). Recognizing which pattern you are seeing hints at the attacker's intent — finding all the web servers versus deeply profiling one chosen victim.

Rogue devices and anomalous traffic

A rogue device is unauthorized hardware on the network — an attacker's drop box, an unsanctioned access point, or an evil-twin AP. It surfaces as an unknown MAC/IP, a new DHCP lease, or unexpected ARP activity. Anomalous activity is any deviation from a learned baseline: a workstation that normally talks only to internal servers suddenly initiating outbound TLS to a foreign IP at 3 a.m. ARP anomalies deserve special note — a sudden change in the MAC associated with the default gateway's IP is the signature of ARP spoofing, a man-in-the-middle technique that lets an attacker intercept local traffic.

IndicatorWhat it suggests
One source → many ports/hostsScanning / enumeration
Traffic on unexpected portsC2 over non-standard port, tunneling
Large outbound transfer off-hoursData exfiltration
Unknown MAC / new APRogue device
Beaconing at fixed intervalsC2 callback
Gateway MAC suddenly changesARP spoofing / MITM

Activity on unexpected ports

Malware frequently hides on ports that are open through the firewall but not associated with the traffic actually carried — for example, a non-HTTP binary protocol riding on TCP 443, or DNS used as a tunnel (DNS tunneling) where unusually long or high-volume TXT queries smuggle data. The mismatch between the port and the protocol's true content is the indicator; deep packet inspection or protocol analyzers reveal it. Attackers favor 443 and 53 precisely because firewalls almost always allow them outbound, so the analyst inspects the content, not just the port — a TLS connection with no valid handshake, or DNS queries that carry encoded payloads rather than resolving real names.

Beaconing and C2 channels

Beaconing is the regular, fixed-interval callback an implant makes to its command-and-control server to fetch instructions. It is one of the most reliable C2 indicators because legitimate software rarely produces perfectly periodic connections to the same destination. Sophisticated implants add jitter — random variation in the interval — to evade simple periodicity detection, so analysts look at the statistical regularity of connections to a destination over time rather than a fixed clock. Tools like Zeek's connection logs make this analysis tractable by recording every connection's timing, duration, and byte counts for later aggregation.

Data exfiltration

Exfiltration shows as outbound volume that breaks the normal inbound-heavy pattern of most clients: large transfers to cloud storage or unknown hosts, transfers timed for off-hours, or steady low-and-slow trickles designed to stay under DLP thresholds. The directionality is the clue — most client machines download far more than they upload, so a workstation pushing gigabytes outbound is intrinsically suspicious regardless of destination. Combining volume, direction, timing, and destination reputation produces a high-confidence exfiltration finding from individually weak signals. Attackers also disguise exfiltration as legitimate traffic — pushing data to a sanctioned cloud-storage provider, or splitting a large dataset into many small DNS or HTTPS requests — so the analyst weighs the destination's legitimacy alongside the volume: a gigabyte to a well-known backup service may be policy, while the same volume to a freshly registered domain is almost certainly theft.

Scan patternShape on the wireAttacker intent
Horizontal scanOne port across many hostsFind a specific vulnerable service
Vertical scanMany ports on one hostProfile a single chosen target
SYN scanSYNs without completed handshakesStealthy port discovery
EnumerationRepeated directory-service queriesExtract users, shares, versions

Combining individually weak signals is what turns a hunch into a high-confidence exfiltration finding:

  • Direction — a client uploading far more than it downloads is intrinsically suspicious.
  • Volume — gigabytes outbound that break the host's baseline.
  • Timing — transfers scheduled for off-hours when no one is working.
  • Destination — reputation of the endpoint (sanctioned backup vs freshly registered domain).
Baseline first

Every "anomaly" is defined against a baseline. Without knowing what normal traffic volume, timing, and destinations look like for a host, you cannot reliably call anything anomalous. Building and maintaining baselines is foundational detection work.

Exam tip

Fixed-interval callbacks = beaconing / C2. Long unusual DNS TXT queries = DNS tunneling / exfiltration. One host hitting many ports = scanning. Gateway MAC suddenly changing = ARP spoofing. Match the traffic shape to the behavior.

Scenario

A finance workstation makes a 0.5 MB HTTPS connection to the same external IP every 60 seconds, 24 hours a day. The perfect regularity and the unusual destination point to beaconing. The analyst pulls the process responsible from EDR, confirms a C2 implant, and isolates the host.

title: Host-Related Indicators of Compromise
html:
When network indicators point at a host, the analyst pivots to endpoint evidence. Host indicators of compromise (IoCs) are observable artifacts that an attacker was — or is — present: anomalous resource use, new software and accounts, abuse of built-in tools, and changes to the file system, registry, or configuration. The richest host telemetry comes from process-creation logging with full command lines, which is why deploying Sysmon or enabling command-line auditing is one of the highest-value detection investments a SOC can make.

Resource consumption

Sudden, unexplained CPU, memory, disk, or bandwidth spikes are classic IoCs. Cryptomining malware pins CPU/GPU at full utilization; ransomware causes intense disk activity as it encrypts files; a data-staging tool fills disk before exfiltration. The deviation from the host's normal resource profile — not the absolute number — is the signal. A build server running at 100% CPU may be normal; a receptionist's workstation doing the same at 3 a.m. is not. Resource anomalies are often the symptom users report first ("my computer is slow"), giving the analyst an entry point into a deeper investigation.

Unauthorized software and accounts

New software the change process never approved, a remote-access tool (AnyDesk, a rogue RDP) the user did not install, or a freshly created local administrator account are strong indicators. Attackers create accounts and add scheduled tasks or services for persistence, ensuring access survives a reboot or a password reset. Legitimate remote-access tools are a favorite because they look like sanctioned IT software and may already be allow-listed — the analyst distinguishes them by who installed them, when, and whether they appear in the approved-software inventory.

LOLBins and malicious scripts

Living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) are legitimate, signed system tools — PowerShell, certutil, mshta, rundll32, wmic, bitsadmin — abused to download payloads, execute code, or move laterally while blending in with normal admin activity. Because the binaries are trusted, detection focuses on how they are invoked: certutil downloading a file, PowerShell with an encoded command, or regsvr32 reaching out to the internet. The defensive value of full command-line logging is precisely here — the binary's reputation is clean, so only the arguments reveal the abuse.

Host IoCLikely meaning
Pegged CPU/GPUCryptominer
Mass file rewrites + new extensionsRansomware
New admin account / servicePersistence
certutil/PowerShell downloadingLOLBin abuse
Run key / scheduled task addedPersistence mechanism
Unsigned binary in Temp/AppDataDropped payload

File system and registry changes

Defenders watch for new or modified files in system directories, executables dropped in user-writable folders (Temp, AppData), and changes to autorun locations: Windows Run/RunOnce keys, services, and scheduled tasks; on Linux, cron jobs, systemd units, and ~/.bashrc. File integrity monitoring (FIM) flags unexpected changes to critical files. The combination of "unsigned executable" plus "writable user directory" plus "new autorun entry pointing to it" is a near-textbook description of malware installing persistence, and any one of those locations is worth alerting on.

Malicious processes and persistence techniques

A malicious process often reveals itself by an unusual parent-child relationship — Word spawning PowerShell, or a browser spawning cmd.exe — or by a trusted name running from the wrong path. Process-creation logs (Sysmon Event ID 1, Windows 4688) and the full command line are the analyst's richest host evidence. Beyond simple autorun keys, attackers use stealthier persistence: WMI event subscriptions that trigger code on a condition, DLL search-order hijacking that loads a malicious library into a trusted process, and registry-resident or fileless payloads that leave little on disk. Knowing these techniques tells the analyst where to look when the obvious Run keys are clean. Process injection deserves special mention: malware injects its code into a legitimate running process (such as explorer.exe) so that, in a process list, only a trusted name appears while the malicious code executes inside it — detection then relies on memory analysis or EDR behavioral telemetry rather than a suspicious file on disk.

Anti-forensics and rootkits

Capable attackers actively work to defeat the analyst. Rootkits hook the operating system to hide their files, processes, and network connections from standard tools, so a process that is plainly running may not appear in Task Manager or ps; detecting it requires comparing kernel-level views against user-level views, or analyzing a memory image with a tool like Volatility. Other anti-forensic techniques include timestomping (altering a file's MAC times to blend in with legitimate system files), clearing or disabling logs, and deleting prefetch and shellbag artifacts. The lesson for triage is that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — when a host behaves as though compromised but the obvious artifacts are clean, the analyst escalates to memory and timeline analysis rather than concluding the host is clean.

When obvious artifacts look clean but a host still behaves as compromised, escalate through stealthier checks:

  1. Diff a kernel-level process view against the user-level view to expose rootkit hiding.
  2. Capture and analyze a memory image (Volatility) for injected or fileless code.
  3. Inspect WMI event subscriptions and DLL search-order paths for non-obvious persistence.
  4. Build a timeline and watch for timestomping — MAC times that do not fit the install history.
Persistence mechanismWhere to look
Run / RunOnce keysHKLM/HKCU ...\Run
Scheduled task / serviceTask Scheduler, services.exe
WMI event subscriptionWMI repository
Linux cron / systemd/etc/cron*, systemd units
Exam tip

A trusted, signed Windows binary used in an unusual way (certutil downloading, PowerShell with -enc) is LOLBin abuse / living off the land — not unknown malware. Detection keys on the command line and parent process, not the file's reputation.

Scenario

Sysmon shows winword.exe spawning powershell.exe with a Base64-encoded command that downloads a file to AppData and adds a Run key. The parent-child relationship alone is the red flag — Word should not launch PowerShell. The analyst confirms a malicious macro, isolates the host, and hunts the same parent-child pattern across the fleet.

title: Application, Cloud, Identity, and Email Indicators
html:
Beyond hosts and packets, attacks surface in application logs, cloud control planes, identity systems, and email. These indicators are increasingly where modern intrusions live, because so much of the enterprise has moved to SaaS and federated identity, and an attacker no longer needs to touch a traditional host to do real damage — stealing a token or abusing an API can be enough.

Application anomalies and service disruption

Application IoCs include spikes in HTTP 500 errors, malformed inputs hitting parameters (SQL metacharacters, path-traversal sequences), unexpected admin-function calls, and outright service disruption such as a denial-of-service flood or a crash loop. Web server and WAF logs reveal injection and traversal attempts as patterns in the request strings. Specific patterns map to specific attacks: ' OR 1=1-- in a parameter signals SQL injection, ../../ sequences signal directory traversal, and script tags in input fields signal cross-site scripting attempts. A burst of 500 errors immediately after such inputs suggests the application is being actively probed and may be breaking under the attack.

Cloud-based attacks

Cloud compromise often targets the control plane rather than a host: an attacker with stolen API keys spins up expensive instances (cryptojacking, visible as a billing spike), opens a storage bucket to public, disables logging (CloudTrail tampering), or creates a backdoor IAM user. The telemetry lives in cloud audit logs, and unusual API calls from a new region or new user agent are key indicators. A particularly important signal is the attacker disabling or deleting logging early in the intrusion — a StopLogging or trail-deletion API call is both an attack action and, paradoxically, one of the last events the log will capture, making it a high-priority alert to wire up.

DomainIndicator
Application500-error spike, injection patterns in requests
CloudNew IAM user, disabled logging, billing spike
IdentityImpossible travel, MFA fatigue, spray attempts
EmailBEC, lookalike domain, mismatched reply-to

Identity / account compromise

Identity indicators include many failed logins followed by a success (brute force/spray succeeding), logins from anomalous geography or device, repeated MFA prompts (MFA fatigue), and impossible travel — the same account authenticating from two locations too far apart to travel between in the elapsed time. Impossible travel is a high-fidelity UEBA detection because it is hard to produce legitimately. Note the difference between brute force (many passwords against one account, which triggers lockout) and password spraying (one common password against many accounts, which evades lockout by spreading attempts thin) — the log signature differs and so does the appropriate detection rule.

Token theft and OAuth abuse

As MFA adoption rises, attackers shift from stealing passwords to stealing the session tokens issued after authentication, because a valid token bypasses MFA entirely. Adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits proxy the real login page, capture the post-MFA cookie, and replay it. Separately, malicious OAuth application consent — tricking a user into granting a rogue app broad mailbox or file permissions — gives persistent access that survives password resets. Indicators include a session token used from a new IP or device shortly after issuance, and unexpected enterprise-app consent grants in the identity provider's audit log.

Email and social engineering

Business email compromise (BEC) uses a hijacked or spoofed executive identity to direct fraudulent wire transfers, typically with urgency and secrecy and a changed reply-to. Related social-engineering indicators include typosquatting (lookalike domains like paypa1.com), URL shorteners hiding the true destination, and display-name spoofing. Email authentication failures — SPF, DKIM, DMARC — are concrete signals that a message did not originate where it claims. The analyst examining a suspicious email reads the full headers: the actual sending IP, the authentication results, the path the message took, and any mismatch between the display name, the From address, and the Reply-To. Two domain tricks recur: homoglyph attacks substitute visually identical characters (a Cyrillic "a" for a Latin one) so the domain looks legitimate to the eye, and cousin domains append a plausible suffix (company-support.com) that passes a casual glance. Reading headers and inspecting the true sending domain, rather than trusting the displayed name, is the durable defense.

Triaging a suspicious email comes down to reading the full headers in a fixed order:

  1. Check the actual sending IP and the path the message took.
  2. Read the SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication results.
  3. Compare the display name, the From address, and the Reply-To for mismatch.
  4. Inspect the true sending domain for homoglyph or cousin-domain tricks.
Email checkWhat it verifies
SPFSending IP is authorized
DKIMMessage signature is valid
DMARCAlignment + policy on failure
Reply-To mismatchReplies redirected to attacker
SPF / DKIM / DMARC

SPF checks the sending IP against an allowed list; DKIM verifies a cryptographic signature; DMARC ties them together and tells receivers what to do on failure. A DMARC failure on a message claiming to be from your CEO is a strong BEC/spoofing indicator.

Exam tip

"Same user, two distant locations within minutes" = impossible travel. "Repeated push prompts until the user approves" = MFA fatigue. "Urgent wire transfer from the CEO with a changed reply-to" = BEC. "One password tried against many accounts" = password spraying.

Scenario

A user reports approving an MFA push they did not initiate. Logs show dozens of push prompts in five minutes followed by an approval and a login from a foreign IP. This is MFA fatigue leading to account compromise; the analyst revokes sessions, resets credentials, and recommends number-matching MFA to stop blind approvals.

title: Packet and Network Analysis Tools
html:
Objective 1.3 names specific tools by category, and the exam expects you to know which tool answers which question. This section covers packet capture and analysis, network-based intrusion detection rule engines, and reputation/attribution services. The recurring exam pattern presents a need — read a conversation, detect a known pattern, enrich an indicator — and asks for the single tool best fit to it, so the goal is to internalize each tool's sweet spot rather than memorize feature lists.

Packet capture: Wireshark and tcpdump

tcpdump is a command-line capture tool ideal for headless servers and quick filtered captures with BPF syntax (tcpdump -i eth0 port 53). Wireshark is the graphical analyzer for deep inspection: it reassembles streams, decodes hundreds of protocols, and lets you "Follow TCP Stream" to read an entire conversation. Display filters (http.request.method == "POST", ip.addr == 10.0.0.5) narrow a noisy capture to the relevant packets. A crucial distinction trips up newcomers: tcpdump and Wireshark use capture filters (BPF, applied before storage to limit what is recorded) and Wireshark additionally has display filters (applied after capture to hide what you do not currently want to see). Capturing broadly and filtering on display is the safer workflow when you may not yet know what matters.

IDS/IPS rule engines

Snort and Suricata are signature-based engines that match traffic against rules and alert or block. A Snort rule has an action, protocol, addresses/ports, a direction operator, and options specifying content to match — analysts read and write these to detect known patterns. Zeek (formerly Bro) takes a different approach: rather than pattern-matching, it produces rich connection and protocol logs (conn.log, dns.log, http.log) that fuel hunting and behavioral analysis. The key conceptual split is signature detection (Snort/Suricata: catches known-bad patterns, blind to novel attacks) versus behavioral/metadata detection (Zeek: records everything for after-the-fact hunting, catches the unknown but requires analysis). Mature SOCs run both.

ToolTypeBest for
tcpdumpCLI captureQuick filtered captures on servers
WiresharkGUI analyzerDeep packet/stream inspection
Snort / SuricataSignature IDS/IPSDetecting/blocking known patterns
ZeekNetwork metadata loggerHunting on connection logs
NetFlow / IPFIXFlow metadataVolume/talker analysis at scale

Reading a Snort rule

Consider alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 445 (msg:"SMB exploit attempt"; content:"|FF|SMB"; sid:1000001;). The action is alert, it matches TCP to the home network on port 445, the msg labels the alert, content specifies the byte pattern to match (the pipe-delimited |FF| is a hex byte), and sid uniquely identifies the rule. Being able to parse these fields — header (action, protocol, source, direction, destination) and body (the options in parentheses) — is a frequent exam task. The direction operator -> matters: it defines which side is source and which is destination, so reversing it changes what the rule catches.

Flow data versus full packet capture

Full packet capture preserves every byte but is storage-expensive and impractical to retain network-wide for long. Flow data (NetFlow, IPFIX) records only metadata about each conversation — source, destination, ports, byte and packet counts, timing — at a tiny fraction of the size, making it feasible to keep across the whole network for long periods. The trade-off is content: flow data tells you that host A sent 4 GB to host B on port 443 for an hour (enough to spot exfiltration or beaconing) but not what was sent. Analysts use flow data for broad, long-horizon detection and reach for full packet capture only on targeted segments when content matters. Where the sensor sits also matters: a SPAN port mirrors switch traffic to a monitoring port and is easy to configure but can drop frames under heavy load, while a passive network tap copies traffic at the physical layer with no loss and no risk to the production link — for high-assurance or OT monitoring, the tap is preferred precisely because it cannot interfere with the traffic it observes.

Reputation and attribution services

To assess an indicator, analysts query reputation and registration services. WHOIS reveals domain registration details (registrar, dates, sometimes registrant); a domain registered yesterday is suspicious. AbuseIPDB aggregates community abuse reports for an IP. GeoIP maps an IP to a physical location, supporting impossible-travel and unexpected-geography findings. None is definitive alone — they are enrichment that raises or lowers confidence, and an analyst combines several (a newly registered domain, hosted in a high-abuse range, resolving to an IP with prior reports) to build a defensible verdict rather than relying on any single lookup.

AspectFull packet captureFlow data (NetFlow/IPFIX)
ContentEvery byte of the payloadMetadata only (no payload)
Storage costVery highTiny fraction
Retention horizonShort, targeted segmentsLong, network-wide
Best forReading the actual conversationVolume/talker and beaconing trends

Choosing a network tool follows the question being asked:

  • Read the actual bytes of a conversation → Wireshark Follow Stream.
  • Grab a quick filtered capture on a headless server → tcpdump with BPF.
  • Detect a known-bad pattern inline → Snort or Suricata signature.
  • Hunt over rich connection logs → Zeek.
  • See volume and top talkers network-wide → NetFlow/IPFIX.
Capture vs display filters

A capture filter (BPF) decides what gets recorded and cannot be undone — you lose what you did not capture. A display filter only hides packets in an existing capture. When in doubt, capture broadly and filter on display.

Exam tip

Need to read the actual bytes of a conversation → Wireshark Follow Stream. Need a quick capture on a server → tcpdump. Need to detect a known pattern in traffic → Snort/Suricata signature. Need rich connection logs for hunting → Zeek. Need volume/talker stats network-wide → NetFlow.

title: SIEM, Threat Intelligence Platforms, and Endpoint/File/Sandbox Tools
html:
The SOC's analytical backbone is a stack of platforms: a SIEM to centralize and correlate logs, threat-intelligence platforms to enrich indicators, EDR/XDR to investigate and contain endpoints, and file-analysis plus sandbox tools to understand suspicious artifacts safely. Knowing which platform answers which question — and how they feed each other — is the difference between a coordinated investigation and a pile of disconnected tools.

SIEM

A Security Information and Event Management platform ingests logs from across the environment, normalizes them, and runs correlation rules that turn many raw events into a single meaningful alert — for example, tying a failed-login burst to a subsequent success and a privilege change into one detection. Analysts pivot, search, and build dashboards in the SIEM; it is the primary triage surface. Tuning correlation rules to reduce false positives is continuous work. SIEM detection broadly splits into correlation rules (deterministic logic on known patterns) and increasingly analytics/UEBA (statistical baselines that flag deviation). The SIEM is also where most metrics live — mean time to detect, alert volume, false-positive rate — making it both the detection engine and the SOC's scorecard. A practical operational reality is the cost model: most commercial SIEMs price on ingestion volume, so analysts and engineers continually decide which sources are worth ingesting, which to sample, and which to keep in cheaper storage — a decision that directly shapes detection coverage and is therefore a security choice, not merely a budget one.

Log sources and the value of correlation

A SIEM's power comes entirely from the breadth and quality of what feeds it. High-value sources include authentication logs, process-creation events, firewall and proxy logs, DNS, endpoint telemetry, and cloud audit trails. Correlation across these is what turns weak individual signals into a strong detection: a failed-login burst (auth log) plus a success from a new country (auth + GeoIP enrichment) plus a privilege change (directory log) plus an unusual outbound connection (firewall log) is, individually, four mundane events, but correlated in sequence it is a textbook account-takeover-to-exfiltration chain. Writing and maintaining these correlation rules — and continuously tuning them against false positives — is the core engineering work behind an effective SIEM.

A textbook account-takeover-to-exfiltration chain is four mundane events that only become a detection when correlated in sequence:

  1. A failed-login burst in the authentication log.
  2. A successful login from a new country (auth log plus GeoIP enrichment).
  3. A privilege change in the directory log.
  4. An unusual outbound connection in the firewall log.

Threat intelligence platforms

TIPs aggregate and operationalize threat data. MISP is an open platform for sharing structured indicators and events among trusted communities. OpenCTI models intelligence as connected entities (actors, campaigns, TTPs) for richer analysis. OTX (Open Threat Exchange) is a community feed of indicator "pulses." These feeds enrich SIEM data so an analyst sees that an observed IP is already known-bad. Intelligence sharing often uses the STIX data format and the TAXII transport protocol, the standards that let platforms exchange structured indicators automatically rather than passing spreadsheets by email.

ToolCategoryUse
SIEMCorrelation/searchCentralized triage and detection
MISP / OpenCTI / OTXThreat intelIndicator sharing and enrichment
EDR / XDREndpoint responseInvestigate, isolate, remediate hosts
YARAFile analysisPattern-match files for malware
Cuckoo / Joe SandboxSandboxDetonate samples safely

EDR and XDR

Endpoint Detection and Response records process, file, registry, and network activity on endpoints, detects malicious behavior, and gives the analyst response actions — notably host isolation, which cuts a compromised machine off the network while preserving it for investigation. XDR (Extended Detection and Response) unifies endpoint, network, email, and cloud telemetry under one correlated platform for broader detection. The practical superpower of EDR is the retrospective query: when a new indicator emerges, the analyst can ask the entire endpoint fleet "has any host ever run this hash or contacted this domain?" and get an answer in seconds — turning a single new IoC into an instant fleet-wide hunt.

File analysis and sandboxing
